signals.title: [docs] Replace Unicode punctuation inside copyable code blocks with ASCII
signals.text: ## Summary Replaces Unicode punctuation inside copyable code blocks with plain ASCII, across five doc pages. Readers copy code blocks into a shell or an editor. A smart quote that looks like a string delimiter, or an en dash that looks like a hyphen, is a syntax error waiting to happen and a confusing one to debug, because the character renders almost identically to the ASCII form it isn't. `rllib-advanced-api.rst` is the clearest case. A class path wrapped in curly double quotes sits two lines above the real `"type": "EpsilonGreedy"` entry it describes: ```python # Exploration sub-class by name or full path to module+class # (e.g., "ray.rllib.utils.exploration.epsilon_greedy.EpsilonGreedy") "type": "EpsilonGreedy", ``` Anyone copying the commented form as a starting point gets an invalid literal. ## What changed | File | Fix | |---|---| | `rllib/rllib-advanced-api.rst` | Curly double quotes to straight, around a class path in a Python comment | | `data/saving-data.rst` | Curly apostrophe to none (reworded); box-drawing comment banner to a plain comment | | `train/user-guides/asynchronous-validation.rst` | Em dash to a sentence break, in a Python comment | | `train/user-guides/data-loading-preprocessing.rst` | Same, in the parallel snippet | | `ray-contribute/dependency-management.md` | Em dash to a sentence break, in a Bash comment | ## What deliberately stayed Scope is punctuation inside code blocks that has a plain ASCII equivalent. Prose is untouched, since em dashes read fine there and Ray's style guide doesn't ban them. Captured program output stayed as-is even inside code blocks, because it's a reproduction rather than something to copy and run: - Box-drawing table borders in `testoutput` blocks in `data/saving-data.rst`, `data/quickstart.rst`, and `ray-contribute/writing-code-snippets.md`. These are compared against real output, so changing them breaks the doctest. - Progress-bar labels using a single-character ellipsis in `serve/tutorials/aws-neuron-core-inference.md`. - Directory-tree diagrams in `serve/tutorials/triton-server-integration.md`, which use non-breaking spaces for alignment. - The verbatim GSM8K prompt in `cluster/kubernetes/examples/verl-post-training.md`. Normalizing its apostrophe would misquote the dataset. ## Verification The affected `testcode` blocks parse identically as Python before and after the change, so nothing that ran before stops running. Vale passes on the changed files.

signals.title: [ci][doc] Log builder CPU and memory around the RtD Sphinx build
signals.text: ## Summary Read the Docs builds intermittently fail with a bare `EOFError` raised from `multiprocessing/connection.py`, with no document named and no cause given: ``` Traceback ========= File ".../multiprocessing/connection.py", line 399, in _recv raise EOFError EOFError make: *** [Makefile:91: html] Error 2 ``` `doc/Makefile` builds with `-j auto`, so Sphinx forks one write worker per CPU. When a worker dies, the parent reports only that `EOFError`. This PR wraps the existing `make` invocation in the `.readthedocs.yaml` html job so the builder's CPU count, cgroup memory ceiling, peak memory, and cgroup OOM counters print around every build. It's a measurement step, not a fix. Nothing about the build changes. ## Why this isn't a content problem - The point in the write phase where it surfaces moves between builds: 58%, 78%, and 92% across three recent failures. A bad document would fail at the same place every time. - Five builds in the last two days failed with this signature, one of them on `master`. Every other RtD failure in that window is an ordinary `fail_on_warning` trip. - One PR hit it after passing an hour earlier on the same base commit, and other PRs built successfully in the same window. | Build | When (UTC) | Version | Died at | |---|---|---|---| | 4343286 | Aug 20 21:52 | PR preview | 58% | | 4343129 | Aug 20 21:11 | PR preview | 92% | | 4343048 | Aug 20 20:59 | PR preview | — | | 4342961 | Aug 20 20:35 | PR preview | — | | 4339216 | Aug 20 03:41 | `master` | 78% | ## Why measure before capping `-j` The likely mechanism is the kernel OOM-killing a write worker. Lowering `-j` is the obvious response, but choosing a value blind would cost wall-clock on every doc build and might buy nothing, since the useful cap depends on how many CPUs the builder actually has. If the builder has two CPUs, `-j auto` is already 2 and a cap isn't the answer at all. The cgroup `memory.events` OOM counters settle whether an OOM kill is even what's happening. ## Implementation notes - The diagnostics run around the build rather than in a `post_build` job because `post_build` is skipped when the build fails, and the failing build is the one worth measuring. - `rc` carries `make`'s exit status through to the job's exit, so a real Sphinx failure still fails the build. Verified under `sh -e` that the diagnostics run and the non-zero status propagates. - Every probe is guarded with `|| true` or `|| echo`, so a missing file or a non-matching `grep` can't abort the job under `set -e`. - The script avoids the constructs the RtD job runner is known to mishandle, per the existing comments in this file: no `printf` with escape sequences, no backslash escapes, and no shell comments inside the block. - Validated with `sh -n` and by parsing the YAML. ## Follow-up Once a few builds have reported their numbers, this wrapper comes back out along with whatever the real fix turns out to be.

signals.title: [core][sandbox] Add an experimental HTTP API service for Ray Sandbox
signals.text: ## Why are these changes needed? Ray Sandbox (`ray.experimental.sandbox`) can currently only be driven from inside the cluster as Ray actors. This PR adds an **experimental HTTP API service** so sandboxes can be managed from outside the cluster with nothing but an HTTP client and a bearer token — for example as an Anyscale service, or from agent-evaluation frameworks (a Harbor `ray-sandbox` environment built on this API is submitted alongside: harbor-framework/harbor PR to follow). This is the second step of the plan from #65570 (first: make the Python API run Docker-built images out of the box; second: make Ray Sandbox consumable as a standalone service). ## Design ``` client ──HTTP/bearer──▶ FastAPI on Ray Serve (ray.experimental.sandbox.http, stateless replicas) │ ray.get_actor(name, namespace) ▼ SandboxHost — named, detached actor per sandbox │ composes SandboxRuntime ▼ gVisor (runsc) on the node ``` - **Named detached actors are the registry.** Any replica resolves any sandbox by name; list = `ray.util.list_named_actors`. The service keeps no state, so replicas scale/restart freely. - **Async submit + poll.** Image pulls and commands outlive HTTP requests and LB limits, so `POST /sandboxes` and `POST .../execs` return `202` immediately; clients poll, optionally long-polling with `wait_seconds` (≤ 30 s per request). Boot progress is observable: `pending → pulling → starting → running | error`. - **One TTL owner.** The API's TTL reclaims the sandbox **and** its hosting actor (the core runtime TTL is deliberately disabled here); an abandoned sandbox never strands an actor reservation. - **Everything sandbox-behavioral is the core `SandboxConfig`'s** (#65570): capabilities (default `DOCKER_DEFAULT_CAPABILITIES`, sets written exactly), network modes (validated against `VALID_NETWORK_MODES`, so a new mode needs no API change), `dns`, `shell` (sandbox-level and per-exec override), and the workdir/readonly writability contract. The API patches nothing. - **Auth**: `Authorization: Bearer <token>` enforced when `RAY_SANDBOX_API_TOKEN` is set; an Anyscale service can leave it unset because the platform edge already requires the service bearer token. `GET /health` is always open. - **Isolation from core**: importing `ray.experimental.sandbox.http` requires `ray[serve]`; the base sandbox package never imports it. Endpoints (`/api/v1`): create/list/get/delete sandboxes, start/poll execs, PUT/GET files, JSON error envelope (`401/404/409/400/413/422/500`). Full table in the new docs section. ## E2E validation Deployed as an Anyscale service (runsc-equipped cluster image) and as a local `serve run`; drove real gVisor sandboxes through create → exec → file transfer → delete, including a full Harbor evaluation run (oracle agent, reward 1.0) against the service URL + token. ## Related issue number Follow-up to #65570. ## Checks - [x] I've signed off every commit (DCO). - [x] I've run pre-commit hooks (`ruff`, `pydoclint`, docstyle, semgrep, import order) on the changed files. - [ ] Unit tests: 54 tests run with **no cluster and no runsc** (fake runtime + fake resolver + FastAPI `TestClient`), including an OpenAPI **contract snapshot** that pins the v1 surface; `test_http_integration.py` is gated on the sandbox test env + `runsc` like the existing sandbox tests. `BUILD.bazel` uses the same `sandbox_tests`/`team:core` tags so the existing CI job picks the package up. - [x] Release tests: N/A (experimental, off by default; nothing imports this package unless deployed).

signals.title: [ci] Give whl_library a pip that can read a JSON index
signals.text: ## What Declares `pypi__pip` at **pip 23.3.2** in `WORKSPACE`, ahead of the one `rules_python` brings, so the pip `whl_library` shells out to can read a PEP 691 JSON simple index. ## Why An index page served as JSON is skipped rather than parsed, and the resolve then fails as though the package did not exist: ``` Skipping page .../simple/pygments/ because the GET request got Content-Type: application/vnd.pypi.simple.v1+json. The only supported Content-Type is text/html ERROR: Could not find a version that satisfies the requirement pygments==2.16.1 (from versions: none) ``` `rules_python` arrives transitively — protobuf's `protobuf_deps()` pins it at **0.14.0** — and 0.14.0 bundles **pip 22.2.1**, one release before JSON support landed in 22.3. The error wording is itself the version tell: pip phrases it that way only while it lacks PEP 691. This matters for the CI mirror. It caches an index page keyed on URL while PyPI answers `Vary: Accept`, so whichever client warms an entry fixes the representation for every later reader — uv asks for JSON, this pip can only read HTML. `ci/pypi_index_proxy.py` pins the upstream request to HTML for exactly that reason (#65593), but pinning producers only holds while every producer cooperates, and it cannot evict an entry already stored. **A pip that reads JSON reads HTML too**, so moving this one forward makes the representation stop mattering in either direction, which is a property rather than a convention. ## Why override one wheel instead of bumping rules_python `pip_install_dependencies()` declares its deps through `maybe()`, which skips any repository that already exists — so declaring `pypi__pip` earlier wins, and the blast radius is the single pip bazel shells out to for python dependency extraction. A `rules_python` bump would be a migration, not a bump: this WORKSPACE uses `pip_install_dependencies`, the `interpreter` symbol from `@python3_10`, and `pip_parse` attributes that all changed after 0.14.0, and newer `rules_python` drops the WORKSPACE mode this build runs in (bazel 7.5.0, `--noenable_bzlmod`). 23.3.2 rather than the newest release: comfortably past 22.3, without pairing a 2022-era `whl_library` with a much later pip CLI. ## Testing ``` $ bazel fetch @pypi__pip//:lib INFO: Analyzed target @@pypi__pip//:lib (7 packages loaded, 537 targets configured). INFO: All external dependencies for the requested targets fetched successfully. $ ls $(bazel info output_base)/external/pypi__pip BUILD.bazel WORKSPACE pip pip-23.3.2.dist-info $ grep ^__version__ $(bazel info output_base)/external/pypi__pip/pip/__init__.py __version__ = "23.3.2" ``` So the override takes precedence over rules_python's 22.2.1 and the generated build file resolves. `buildifier --mode=check WORKSPACE` clean. Wheel URL and sha256 come from the PyPI JSON API for 23.3.2. Observed downstream in rayturbo build 14076 (`pygments==2.16.1`) and fixed there by the same change, anyscale/rayturbo#4217. Not a duplicate: no open PR touches `pypi__pip` or the `rules_python` pin — #65538 and #65567 are unrelated CI work. AI assistance was used for this change.

signal.title: [train] Share PlacementGroupCleaner across Train runs
signal.text: ## Description Ray Train v2 currently creates one detached `PlacementGroupCleaner` actor per Train controller. Since cleaners are pinned to the head node, their memory use grows linearly with concurrent Train runs. In the workload described in #65443, 24 cleaners use approximately 14.4 GB on the head node. This PR replaces the per-controller actors with one cluster-wide shared cleaner. The cleaner tracks controllers independently, so a failed controller only triggers cleanup for its own placement groups. The shared cleaner: - uses a fixed, versioned name and internal namespace with `get_if_exists=True`; - remains detached, pinned to the head node, and scheduled outside captured placement groups; - persists controller and placement-group registrations in GCS internal KV; - restores active and incomplete cleanup records after actor restart; - rejects late placement-group registration after controller death; - isolates State API and placement-group cleanup failures between controllers; - scopes State API queries to its own cluster when multiple clusters are active. ## Related issues Fixes #65443. ## Testing ```text PYTHONPATH="$PWD/python" python -m pytest -q \ python/ray/train/v2/tests/test_placement_group_cleaner.py # 16 passed PYTHONPATH="$PWD/python" python -m pytest -q \ python/ray/train/v2/tests/test_controller_callback_behaviour.py # 10 passed pre-commit run --files \ python/ray/train/v2/_internal/callbacks/placement_group_callback.py \ python/ray/train/v2/_internal/execution/controller/placement_group_cleaner.py \ python/ray/train/v2/_internal/state/util.py \ python/ray/train/v2/tests/test_placement_group_cleaner.py # Passed git diff --check origin/master...HEAD # Passed ``` A local end-to-end multi-job scenario used two independent drivers, each running a real Train v2 `DataParallelTrainer` with a controller, worker, and placement group. Both runs shared one cleaner. After one driver was killed, only its placement group was removed; the other run remained active and completed normally. The cleaner stayed alive throughout. ## Contribution notes No other open PR referencing #65443 or matching this PlacementGroupCleaner change was found before requesting review. AI assistance was used for implementation, testing, and self-review of this change.

signal.title: [docs][core] Document JVM signal conflicts with PyArrow HDFS
signal.text: ## Why are these changes needed? On Linux, PyArrow HDFS loads `libhdfs`, which embeds a HotSpot JVM in the Python process. HotSpot uses some `SIGSEGV` events as recoverable VM control flow, while Ray's CoreWorker installs an Abseil failure-signal handler that can interpret the same signal as a fatal native crash. The conflict can be established during handler installation and surface later as an intermittent JVM crash. This PR documents: - the symptoms and root cause of the Ray/PyArrow HDFS signal-handler conflict; - HotSpot signal chaining with `libjsig.so` as the preferred mitigation because it keeps Ray's native crash diagnostics enabled; - `RAY_DISABLE_FAILURE_SIGNAL_HANDLER=1` as a fallback and its diagnostic trade-off; - the process-start timing requirement for `LD_PRELOAD` and a KubeRay configuration example; - discoverable entry points from the Ray Data and Ray Train HDFS documentation. Related to #36415. ## Duplicate-work check I reviewed #36415 and searched open PRs for the issue number, `libjsig`, and PyArrow/HDFS signal-handler documentation. I found no open PR covering this documentation work. #58984 is already merged and added `RAY_DISABLE_FAILURE_SIGNAL_HANDLER`, but it didn't document the option, its diagnostic trade-off, or HotSpot signal chaining. ## Validation Documentation checks: - `git diff --check` - `python -m pre_commit run --files doc/source/ray-observability/user-guides/debug-apps/debug-failures.rst doc/source/train/user-guides/persistent-storage.rst doc/source/data/loading-data.rst` - `sphinx-lint --disable trailing-whitespace doc/source/ray-observability/user-guides/debug-apps/debug-failures.rst doc/source/train/user-guides/persistent-storage.rst doc/source/data/loading-data.rst` - `./ci/lint/lint.sh documentation_style` (`0 errors, 0 warnings`) - Verified the linked Oracle signal-handling pages and #36415 return HTTP 200. - Validated the documented `find`/`LD_PRELOAD` shell snippet with the local OpenJDK 17.0.19 installation. Runtime validation behind the guidance: - Reproduced the unmitigated JVM termination and generated multiple `hs_err_pid*.log` files. - Completed 5,000- and 10,000-operation HDFS stress runs with `RAY_DISABLE_FAILURE_SIGNAL_HANDLER=1` without reproducing the crash. - Completed a 5,000-operation HDFS stress run with only `libjsig.so` preloaded and Ray's handler left enabled. - Completed a separate 1,000-operation `libjsig.so` run, followed by a clean `ray.shutdown()` and process exit code 0. The full Sphinx documentation site wasn't built locally because the existing Python environment doesn't include the Ray documentation dependency set. The Read the Docs preview build provides full-site validation. ## AI assistance AI assistance was used to investigate the failure, draft the documentation, and run the validation commands. I reviewed every changed line and the reported test results.

signal.text: ## Description As mentioned in the issue 64992. `log_to_driver=True` (the default) prepends a `(name pid=...)` prefix to every worker/actor stdout/stderr line forwarded to the driver. signal.title: [core][sandbox] Add an experimental HTTP API service for Ray Sandbox
signal.text: ## Why are these changes needed? Ray Sandbox (`ray.experimental.sandbox`) can currently only be driven from inside the cluster as Ray actors. This PR adds an **experimental HTTP API service** so sandboxes can be managed from outside the cluster with nothing but an HTTP client and a bearer token — for example as an Anyscale service, or from agent-evaluation frameworks (a Harbor `ray-sandbox` environment built on this API is submitted alongside: harbor-framework/harbor PR to follow). This is the second step of the plan from #65570 (first: make the Python API run Docker-built images out of the box; second: make Ray Sandbox consumable as a standalone service). ## Design ``` client ──HTTP/bearer──▶ FastAPI on Ray Serve (ray.experimental.sandbox.http, stateless replicas) │ ray.get_actor(name, namespace) ▼ SandboxHost — named, detached actor per sandbox │ composes SandboxRuntime ▼ gVisor (runsc) on the node ``` - **Named detached actors are the registry.** Any replica resolves any sandbox by name; list = `ray.util.list_named_actors`. The service keeps no state, so replicas scale/restart freely. - **Async submit + poll.** Image pulls and commands outlive HTTP requests and LB limits, so `POST /sandboxes` and `POST .../execs` return `202` immediately; clients poll, optionally long-polling with `wait_seconds` (≤ 30 s per request). Boot progress is observable: `pending → pulling → starting → running | error`. - **One TTL owner.** The API's TTL reclaims the sandbox **and** its hosting actor (the core runtime TTL is deliberately disabled here); an abandoned sandbox never strands an actor reservation. - **Everything sandbox-behavioral is the core `SandboxConfig`'s** (#65570): capabilities (default `DOCKER_DEFAULT_CAPABILITIES`, sets written exactly), network modes (validated against `VALID_NETWORK_MODES`, so a new mode needs no API change), `dns`, `shell` (sandbox-level and per-exec override), and the workdir/readonly writability contract. The API patches nothing. - **Auth**: `Authorization: Bearer <token>` enforced when `RAY_SANDBOX_API_TOKEN` is set; an Anyscale service can leave it unset because the platform edge already requires the service bearer token. `GET /health` is always open. - **Isolation from core**: importing `ray.experimental.sandbox.http` requires `ray[serve]`; the base sandbox package never imports it. Endpoints (`/api/v1`): create/list/get/delete sandboxes, start/poll execs, PUT/GET files, JSON error envelope (`401/404/409/400/413/422/500`). Full table in the new docs section. ## E2E validation Deployed as an Anyscale service (runsc-equipped cluster image) and as a local `serve run`; drove real gVisor sandboxes through create → exec → file transfer → delete, including a full Harbor evaluation run (oracle agent, reward 1.0) against the service URL + token. ## Related issue number Follow-up to #65570. ## Checks - [x] I've signed off every commit (DCO). - [x] I've run pre-commit hooks (`ruff`, `pydoclint`, docstyle, semgrep, import order) on the changed files. - [ ] Unit tests: 54 tests run with **no cluster and no runsc** (fake runtime + fake resolver + FastAPI `TestClient`), including an OpenAPI **contract snapshot** that pins the v1 surface; `test_http_integration.py` is gated on the sandbox test env + `runsc` like the existing sandbox tests. `BUILD.bazel` uses the same `sandbox_tests`/`team:core` tags so the existing CI job picks the package up. - [x] Release tests: N/A (experimental, off by default; nothing imports this package unless deployed).

signal.title: [Core] Store an error when the owner reports an object as FREED
signal.text: ## Description `FutureResolver::ProcessResolvedObject` handles three outcomes of a borrower's `GetObjectStatus` RPC: an unreachable owner stores `OWNER_DIED`, `OUT_OF_SCOPE` stores `OBJECT_DELETED`, and `CREATED` stores the value. `GetObjectStatusReply::ObjectStatus` also has `FREED`, which the owner sends when the object's value was freed while the borrower's reference was still in scope. That status matches no branch, so nothing is put into the memory store and nothing is logged. A `ray.get` on that reference blocks forever with no error. No other path fills the store either. `ResolveFutureAsync` sends one RPC and does not retry. `GetObjects` only falls through to plasma for entries that already exist carrying `IsInPlasmaError`, so a missing entry never gets there. The `OWNER_DIED` put in this function is the only one in the tree, so a later owner death does not help. The pre-ownership raylet code did handle this, treating `FREED` alongside `OUT_OF_SCOPE`: `if (!status.ok() || reply.status() == OUT_OF_SCOPE || reply.status() == FREED) { MarkObjectsAsFailed(OBJECT_UNRECONSTRUCTABLE, ...) }`. That block was deleted wholesale in #14184 and the `FREED` case was never ported to `FutureResolver`. The fix stores `OBJECT_FREED`, which is what the sibling branches do for their statuses. That is also the error the owner already stores locally in `DeleteImpl`, and the one Python maps to `ObjectFreedError`, so the owner and the borrower raise the same exception for the same event. `OBJECT_DELETED` (what the `OUT_OF_SCOPE` sibling uses) would be wrong here, because it maps to `ReferenceCountingAssertionError`, whose message says "This should not happen"; that would report a legitimate user action as an internal Ray invariant violation. ## Related issues Fixes #65269 ## Additional information Adds `future_resolver_test.cc`; this class had no test file. The `FREED` case fails against the unfixed code (nothing is stored, `GetIfExists` returns null) and passes with the fix. I re-verified that by reverting only the production change and re-running. The other two statuses are covered as regression anchors. `bazel test //src/ray/core_worker/tests:future_resolver_test` passes, including under `--config=asan`. Two notes for reviewers. The most familiar trigger, `ray.internal.free`, is deprecated, but the `DeleteObjects` RPC handler and `SealExisting(pin_object=false)` reach the same owner-side freed state and are not. I also left the `if/else` chain as a chain instead of converting it to a `switch` on the enum, to keep this to one concern; a `switch` would stop a future fourth value from being dropped the same way. I used AI assistance to investigate and draft this change. I reviewed every changed line and ran the build and tests myself.

signal.title: [Data] Raise a clear error when _backfill_missing_fields gets a non-struct column
signal.text: ## Description `_align_struct_fields` guards top-level columns with `isinstance(column.type, pa.StructType)`, but its recursive call only checks the *target* field type. So a nested field that is a struct in one block and a primitive in another passed the outer guard and failed inside `_backfill_missing_fields` while iterating `column.type`. `unify_schemas` permits the mismatch: `_reconcile_field` keeps only the struct arms, so the unified type claims `inner` is a struct even though one block holds an `int64`. ``` a = ray.data.from_items([{"c": {"inner": {"y": 1}}}]) b = ray.data.from_items([{"c": {"inner": 5}}]) a.union(b).repartition(1).take_all() # was: TypeError: 'pyarrow.lib.DataType' object is not iterable # now: ValueError: Column of type int64 cannot be aligned with struct type # struct<y: int64>. A block holds a non-struct value where the unified # schema expects a struct. ``` This adds that same check at the top of the function. An all-null nested field infers as `pa.null()` and is filled with nulls of the target type rather than rejected. Raising seemed safer than the issue's other option (backfilling a null struct), since coercing a schema conflict silently alters data — happy to switch. The issue's repro no longer reaches this path: for a *top-level* mismatch the outer guard skips alignment and `pa.concat_tables` raises a readable `ArrowTypeError`. Only the nested case leaked the `TypeError`. ## Related issues Fixes #61656 ## Additional information Tests: the nested mismatch via `_align_struct_fields` and via `concat`, plus the all-null case. `unit/test_transform_pyarrow.py` 81 passed (was 78); `unit/test_arrow_block.py` 66, `test_map.py` 240, `test_union.py` 5, `datasource/test_json.py` 58 passed; `pre-commit` clean; reverting either branch fails its test. Bazel/C++ not run locally. #61656 is unassigned and no open PR touches this file; two earlier attempts (#62170, #63960) were closed by the stale bot without maintainer objection. AI assistance (Claude) was used; I reviewed every changed line and ran the tests above.

signal.title: [job] Eagerly initialize JobManager on head node to fix job recovery …
signal.text: …after restart After the head Dashboard Agent restarts while GCS job metadata still exists, non-terminal submission jobs (PENDING/RUNNING) were not recovered until a subsequent Job API request lazily created the JobManager. This happened because JobAgent.run() was a no-op, and get_job_manager() (which constructs JobManager and schedules _recover_running_jobs()) was only called from HTTP handlers. Fix: on the head node, run() now launches a background task that connects to Ray and eagerly initializes JobManager with exponential backoff retry (1s-60s) to handle GCS still recovering. Worker agents are unchanged. > Thank you for contributing to Ray! 🚀 > Please review the [Ray Contribution Guide](https://docs.ray.io/en/master/ray-contribute/getting-involved.html) before opening a pull request. > ⚠️ Remove these instructions before submitting your PR. > 💡 Tip: Mark as draft if you want early feedback, or ready for review when it's complete. ## Description > Briefly describe what this PR accomplishes and why it's needed. ## Related issues > Link related issues: "Fixes #1234", "Closes #1234", or "Related to #1234". ## Additional information > Optional: Add implementation details, API changes, usage examples, screenshots, etc.

signal.title: [Train] Use user-defined train function name in training thread name and error stack traces
signal.text: ## Description When a user's training function raises an exception, the training thread (and the resulting stack trace) is named after Ray's internal wrapper `train_fn_with_final_checkpoint_flush` instead of the user-defined function. The root cause is in `RayTrainWorker.run_train_fn`: the user's training function is wrapped by an inner `train_fn_with_final_checkpoint_flush` , and this wrapper is what gets handed to `ThreadRunner`. `ThreadRunner` names the training thread via `get_callable_name(target)`, so it reads the wrapper's `__name__` and produces `TrainingThread(train_fn_with_final_checkpoint_flush)`. We apply `functools.wraps(train_fn)` to the inner wrapper so it inherits the user function's `__name__`. This is similar to how `construct_train_func` preserves the user's name on `train_fn` via `functools.wraps`. ## Related issues Fixes TRAIN-744 on Jira ## Testing Added a unit test `test_training_thread_name_matches_user_fn` in `python/ray/train/v2/tests/test_worker.py`. It runs `RayTrainWorker.run_train_fn` with a user function named `my_custom_train_fn` and asserts the launched training thread is named `TrainingThread(my_custom_train_fn)` (rather than `TrainingThread(train_fn_with_final_checkpoint_flush)`). Without the `functools.wraps` fix this assertion fails, so the test guards the fix. ## Reproduction Repro script and before/after logs: https://gist.github.com/avigyabb/626151d1b05526f38b221198f6858c65 The script uses Ray's real `ThreadRunner` and `get_callable_name` and rebuilds the exact wrapper from `worker.py`, toggling `@functools.wraps` to show both states in a single run (no cluster required). It also has an `--e2e` mode that drives the real `DataParallelTrainer`. Results (`thread_name_before_after.log`): | | Thread / stack-trace name | | --- | --- | | **Before fix** | `TrainingThread(train_fn_with_final_checkpoint_flush)` | | **After fix** | `TrainingThread(train_fn_per_worker)` | ## Additional information > Optional: Add implementation details, API changes, usage examples, screenshots, etc.

signal.title: [core][dashboard] Harden agent task supervision and dead-node KV cleanup (Re-opening #63796)
signal.text: **Supersedes closed PR #63796** **Fixes #63574** ### What does this PR do? This PR addresses the feedback from #63796 and reliably fixes the issue where a single dashboard module throwing an exception crashes the entire `DashboardAgent.run()` task. The core issue was that `asyncio.gather` propagates exceptions by default. I fixed this by implementing `run_module_supervised`, which explicitly catches and logs the module exception instead of letting it bubble up, allowing `agent.run()` to gracefully survive module failures. This ensures the Dashboard Agent doesn't stop responding to Kubernetes liveness probes during autoscale-down events. ### Proof of Fix (Verified Locally) To prove this fix is robust and not flaky, I added `test_dashboard_agent_survives_module_exception`. This test explicitly injects a faulty module, asserts that it logs the crash correctly (verified via patching the logger), and guarantees it does not crash the overarching agent loop. Here are the logs of both the new supervision test and the KV cleanup test passing cleanly on my local environment: ```text $ python -m pytest python/ray/dashboard/tests/test_dashboard.py::test_dashboard_agent_survives_module_exception -v ============================= test session starts ============================= platform win32 -- Python 3.11.9, pytest-7.4.4 plugins: anyio-4.12.0, hypothesis-6.98.3, asyncio-0.17.2, timeout-2.1.0 asyncio: mode=Mode.AUTO timeout: 180.0s collecting ... python\ray\dashboard\tests\test_dashboard.py::test_dashboard_agent_survives_module_exception ✓100% ██████████ Results (0.47s): 1 passed $ python -m pytest python/ray/dashboard/modules/node/tests/test_node.py::test_update_node_survives_dead_node_kv_delete_failure -v ============================= test session starts ============================= platform win32 -- Python 3.11.9, pytest-7.4.4 plugins: anyio-4.12.0, hypothesis-6.98.3, asyncio-0.17.2, timeout-2.1.0 asyncio: mode=Mode.AUTO timeout: 180.0s collecting ... python\ray\dashboard\modules\node\tests\test_node.py::test_update_node_survives_dead_node_kv_delete_failure ✓100% ██████████ Results (1.03s): 1 passed

signal.title: [Data] [6/11] Add FooterFileIndexer behind an opt-in flag, with bin packing as a partitioner
signal.text:
## Why Parquet V2 chunks files **blindly**. `ParquetFileChunker` splits each file by `ceil(file_size / 1 GiB)` *without reading the footer*, and `RoundRobinPartitioner` bin-packs those guesses with a fixed encoding-ratio estimate. Bin sizes are inaccurate because the compression ratio is unknown until the footer is read, there is no row-group skipping, and nothing from predicate / limit / projection push-down reaches listing. This wires steps 1–5 into a working read path — the first PR in the split where the footer path is *reachable*. **Default-off.** Gated on `RAY_DATA_PARQUET_ENABLE_FOOTER_INDEXER`; without it every Parquet V2 read behaves exactly as today. Flipping the default and deleting the blind chunker are separate later steps, which keeps this reviewable and leaves a one-line revert lever. ## What this changes **1. `FooterFileIndexer` — listing that reads footers.** New indexer, returned from `_get_file_indexer()` only when the flag is set. It footer-reads files on a `FooterReader` actor pool (step 5) and emits **one listing row per row-group run**, each carrying that run's exact stats: `num_rows`, `uncompressed_size`, per-row-group `rg_sizes` / `rg_rows`, and `fully_matched`. Actor pool is killed in a `finally`, in-flight footer batches are bounded, and listing stops early once `limit` exact-survivor rows are delivered. **2. Bin packing is a `FilePartitioner`, not an indexer detail.** Listing discovers work; the partitioner groups it. `OnlineBinPacker` (step 4) becomes a real `FilePartitioner` supplied via a new `DataSourceV2.get_file_partitioner()` hook, so it runs in the normal partitioner stage and can split runs at exact row-group boundaries. `FileIndexer.produces_partitioned_manifests` is deleted in favor of `FilePartitioner.requires_global_input`, which is what tells `plan_list_files_op` to keep listing on one task. This is not just tidying — it fixes a parallelism bug. `produces_partitioned_manifests` made the planner skip the partitioner stage entirely, so with `shuffle="files"` the footer path read the **whole dataset in a single task**: `shuffle_files` concatenates every sealed bin into one manifest block, and with no partitioner downstream nothing was left to re-split it. **3. `count()` push-down.** `PushdownCountFiles` tried to force whole-file listing by overwriting the indexer's `_file_chunker`, but `FooterFileIndexer` overrides `list_files` outright and ignores its chunker, so the swap was a silent no-op. It now swaps the indexer itself via `as_whole_file_indexer()`. This is what makes (2) safe: once listing emits a row per row-group run, `read_metadata` returns the whole file's row count for *each* row, so a 4-row-group file counts 4×. The hard `assert isinstance(...)` also becomes a debug log and bail-out, so a third-party indexer falls back to the regular read path instead of crashing the optimizer. **4. `skip_paths` on the footer path.** `FooterFileIndexer` was constructed without it, so `read_parquet(..., skip_paths=...)` silently did nothing when the flag was on — excluded files were read, and a path named only in `skip_paths` could fail the listing instead of being ignored. These land together because (3) guards a bug that (2) introduces, and both touch the same listing contract. ## Flow ```mermaid flowchart TD LF[ListFiles] --> FI[FooterFileIndexer] FI --> LI["list_file_infos
(step 1)"] LI --> BA[batch paths] BA --> AP["FooterReaderActor pool
SPREAD (step 5)"] AP -->|one row per row-group run| SH[shuffle_files] SH --> BP["OnlineBinPacker
(step 4), a FilePartitioner"] BP -->|sealed bins| MB[manifest blocks] MB --> RF[ReadFiles] RF --> PR["ParquetFileReader
reads exactly the named row groups"] LF -.->|"predicate / limit / projected_columns
(step 3)"| FI ``` `OnlineBinPacker.requires_global_input = True` keeps listing on a single task, since the packer holds one pool of open bins across all files. ## Files | File | Change | | --- | --- | | `listing/footer_file_indexer.py` | **new** — `FooterFileIndexer`. All knobs re-read in `__init__` so `monkeypatch.setenv` and release-test overrides apply. | | `listing/file_indexer.py` | drops `produces_partitioned_manifests`; adds `as_whole_file_indexer()` | | `partitioners/online_bin_packer.py` | now a `FilePartitioner` (`add_input`, `requires_global_input`) | | `partitioners/file_partitioner.py` | adds `requires_global_input` | | `datasource_v2.py` / `read_api.py` | new `get_file_partitioner()` hook; default stays `RoundRobinPartitioner` | | `parquet_datasource_v2.py` | flag-gated indexer + packer; wires `skip_paths` | | `planner/plan_list_files_op.py` | partitioner stage always runs; single-task listing keys off `requires_global_input` | | `rules/pushdown_count_files.py` | replaces the indexer instead of reconfiguring it | | `chunkers/file_chunker.py` | `ParquetRowGroupChunkMetadata` gains `fully_matched`, `rg_sizes`, `rg_rows` | | `chunkers/parquet_file_chunking_utils.py` | adds `_fragments_from_row_group_ids`, `_with_io_retry` | | `readers/parquet_file_reader.py` | dispatches on metadata type so both chunkers coexist; sizes batches from footer stats already on the manifest | | `readers/file_reader.py` | `_resolve_batch_size(dataset, manifest)` | ## Testing ``` pytest python/ray/data/tests/unit/datasource_v2/test_file_indexer.py \ python/ray/data/tests/unit/datasource_v2/test_online_bin_packer.py \ python/ray/data/_internal/datasource_v2/tests/test_parquet_datasource_v2.py \ python/ray/data/_internal/datasource_v2/tests/test_footer_chunking.py \ python/ray/data/tests/datasource/test_read_parquet_v2.py # 145 passed ``` The two that carry the most weight: - `test_count_matches_rows`, parametrized over `(4 files, 1000 rows, row_group_size=250)`. This is the guard for (3): without `as_whole_file_indexer()` it fails `assert 4800 == 1200`. - `test_e2e_filter_then_limit_with_nulls`, 20 files at 10% non-null over five limits. If a null were ever counted as an exact survivor, listing would stop short and `Limit` would quietly return fewer rows than asked. (The classification behind that landed in #65273.) **Known gap:** `skip_paths` has unit coverage in `test_parquet_datasource_v2.py` but no end-to-end test through `read_parquet` on the footer path. ## Stack Step 6 of an 11-step split of #64985 (43 files, +3234 −719, not reviewable as one unit). - #65167 `[1/11]` `FileIndexer.list_file_infos` ✅ · #65168 `[2/11]` limit into `ReadFiles` ✅ - #65214 `[3/11]` derive `ListFiles` pushdown state ✅ · #65210 `[4/11]` footer types + bin packer ✅ - #65273 `[5/11]` `FooterReader` actor pool ✅ - **this PR** — consumes all of the above; first step that makes the path reachable - #65169 `[9/11]` pin the footer actor pool to 1 in tests (open, independent) This PR **absorbs what was going to be step 7** (`count()` push-down), so the remaining steps renumber down by one. Step 7 can't be split out downstream of this: the packing change is what triggers the over-count, so the fix has to ship at or below it. ## AI assistance AI assistance was used for this change. I have reviewed every changed line and run the tests above locally. Not a duplicate: `gh pr list --repo ray-project/ray --state open --search "FooterFileIndexer"` and `--search "footer indexer parquet"` return only this PR, the stack members listed above, and #64985 — the mega-PR this stack is splitting up, which closes once the stack lands.

signal.title: [core][joblib] Add opt-in autoscaling to ray.util.multiprocessing.Pool
signal.text: ## Description Closes #31128. The Ray Joblib backend uses `ray.util.multiprocessing.Pool`. Historically, that Pool eagerly created a fixed number of actors from the cluster's current CPU count. A zero-CPU head therefore could not express a larger logical concurrency target, create pending resource demand, and scale workers from zero. This PR adds experimental, opt-in Pool autoscaling without adding a second Joblib backend. Supplying any of `min_size`, `max_size`, `initial_size`, or `idle_timeout_s` enables autoscaling; `Pool()` and `Pool(processes=N)` retain fixed-pool behavior. ```python pool = Pool( min_size=0, max_size=64, initial_size=0, idle_timeout_s=60, ray_remote_args={"num_cpus": 1}, ) ``` Pool autoscaling and Ray cluster autoscaling remain separate. Pool actors retain their existing `num_cpus=0` default. Callers must explicitly request resources through `ray_remote_args` when pending actors should create cluster-autoscaler demand. The Joblib backend forwards the same options. `n_jobs` remains its concurrency ceiling, and `max_size` may lower but never raise that ceiling. `RayBackend.configure()` constructs the Ray Pool directly instead of changing Joblib's `PicklingPool` inheritance process-wide. Local multiprocessing memmapping arguments are ignored because Ray transfers values through its object store; supported Pool arguments continue to pass through using installed-version signature detection. ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR Caller["Pool / Joblib callers"] -->|"Submit, FinishProducer, Close, Terminate"| CQ["single FIFO control queue"] Future["ObjectRef.future callbacks"] -->|"immutable completion token only"| CQ CQ --> Controller["single PoolController owner thread"] Controller --> Registry["bounded Joblib ObjectRef cache"] Controller --> Pending["local pending deque"] Controller --> Table["ActorSlotTable"] Table --> Slots["fixed canonical ActorSlot array"] Slots --> Actors["PoolActor processes"] Actors --> Future Controller -->|"Completion(sequence, TaskSuccess/TaskFailure[])"| Port["ResultPort"] Controller -->|"End(expected_completions, terminal_error)"| Port Port --> Collector["isolated ResultThread"] Collector --> Result["AsyncResult / IMapIterator / callbacks"] Caller -.->|"Join: wait for Controller exit"| Controller ``` The control queue order is the linearization order for admission, producer exhaustion, close, terminate, and distributed completions. Those APIs wait only for a local command acknowledgment. `join()` is deliberately not a control command: it checks that the Pool is no longer `RUNNING`, then waits for the Controller thread to converge and verifies terminal cleanup. API threads do not mutate `PoolState`, slot state, or scheduling state. A real Pool never falls back to executing Controller work on an API thread if that thread dies; it fails closed with the Controller's terminal error. Each Ray `ObjectRef` is converted once to its public `Future`. Its callback captures only the control queue, wakeup-free immutable token, and token ID. It never mutates the Pool. The Controller validates token ownership against `(slot index, slot generation, ref kind, ref identity)` before applying a transition. Already-completed Futures, duplicate events, and stale generations are covered explicitly. The control path contains no `ray.wait` polling, periodic ObjectRef polling, READY heap, detached termination registry, or second inbound work queue. Queue timeouts are used only for semantic deadlines: startup retry, idle retirement, graceful-stop escalation, and hard terminal cleanup timeout. Canonical storage remains on `Pool`, while the Controller thread is its sole runtime mutator. `_PoolController` is intentionally small but not redundant: it owns the pending deque, queue/weak-reference lifetime, and thread entry point. Moving every field physically behind that wrapper would add public-API forwarding and weak/strong-reference lifecycle edges without reducing a transition entry. In the current structure, `PoolState` has one transition method, all slot replacement is inside `ActorSlotTable`, `_slots` is a derived read-only view, and Future callbacks can only enqueue immutable tokens. This gives behavioral single ownership without creating a second facade over the public Pool object. ## Actor slot state machine ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> EMPTY EMPTY --> CREATING: created(actor, demand) CREATING --> STARTING: readiness_submitted(ref) STARTING --> READY: readiness Future succeeded STARTING --> EMPTY: actor died READY --> RUNNING: batch_dispatched(ref, port, sequence) READY --> READY: synchronous batch submission failed RUNNING --> READY: batch Future settled RUNNING --> EMPTY: actor died CREATING --> STOPPING: stop ownership committed STARTING --> STOPPING: scale-down or terminal stop READY --> STOPPING: idle, retirement, or terminal stop RUNNING --> STOPPING: retirement or terminal stop state STOPPING { [*] --> StopPending: owns actor before Ray call StopPending --> ExitFutureOwned: exit Future submitted StopPending --> StopPending: submission retry or force ExitFutureOwned --> ExitFutureOwned: graceful stop escalated } STOPPING --> EMPTY: actor-exit Future confirmed ``` `ActorSlot` is a discriminated union of immutable payloads. Readiness, batch, and actor-exit refs cannot occupy the wrong state. Every transition enters through `ActorSlotTable`; Pool code cannot clear or assemble slot fields independently. A stop is committed in the canonical slot before the first Ray termination side effect. The typed pending-stop payload therefore owns the actor even if graceful-stop or kill submission raises synchronously; retry cannot free or reuse the slot. The transition invalidates any superseded readiness/batch completion owner before registering actor-exit ownership. Once the exit Future is registered, the slot remains submitted-`STOPPING` until that Future resolves. Escalation to `ray.kill` changes only the forced flag and preserves generation, actor handle, confirmation ref, and completion token. `CLOSED` and `TERMINATED` are rejected unless every slot is `EMPTY`. This prevents physical actor overlap and makes `join()` a pure wait for Controller convergence rather than a second cleanup owner. Startup failures are counted per parallel startup round, not per actor. A readiness success in a round proves that the Pool can make progress and clears peer failures from that round. Both startup and terminal-cleanup retries have explicit limits independent of `max_size`, so changing capacity cannot silently change the failure policy. ## Accepted operation and result ownership ```mermaid flowchart LR Command["SubmitCommand / atomic SubmitManyCommand"] -->|"Controller accepts + reserves sequence(s)"| Pending["pending deque owns BatchOperation"] Pending -->|"run_batch.remote fails synchronously"| LocalFailure["ResultPort Completion"] Pending -->|"READY -> RUNNING"| Running["RUNNING slot owns ref + port + sequence"] Running -->|"Future settles"| Completion["ResultPort Completion"] Running -->|"terminate / fatal Controller failure"| TerminalCompletion["one terminal Completion"] LocalFailure --> Settled["settled"] Completion --> Settled TerminalCompletion --> Settled ``` Container membership is the operation lifecycle: the control command is awaiting admission, the pending deque owns an accepted operation, the `RUNNING` slot owns a dispatched operation, and `ResultPort` owns a settled result. `(ResultPort identity, sequence)` is the stable operation identity; a second mutable operation ID or lifecycle enum would duplicate this canonical ownership. There is no mutable parallel operation state that can disagree with those containers. Eager `map` chunks use one `SubmitManyCommand`. Reserving every sequence, accepting every operation, and publishing the acknowledgment form one Controller transaction, so a concurrent close observes the map as all accepted or all rejected. Lazy iterators keep their per-chunk admission boundary. The `READY -> RUNNING` transition is the dispatch ownership point. The operation leaves `pending` immediately at that transition, before Future callback registration, so every synchronous failure window has exactly one owner. A submitted but unobservable ref poisons the Pool fail-closed rather than falling back to polling or reusing the actor. Remote values use explicit `TaskSuccess` and `TaskFailure` envelopes. Returning an `Exception` object is successful data. Result callbacks are isolated from collection; callback exceptions are logged without corrupting the authoritative result. ## ResultPort protocol ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant P as Producer / Controller participant R as ResultPort participant C as ResultThread P->>R: reserve sequence at admission P->>R: Completion(sequence, outcomes) P->>R: End(exact reserved count, optional terminal error) Note over R,C: End may arrive before the last Completion C->>C: finish only when received count == End.expected ``` Fixed results know their exact count at construction. Lazy iterators learn it from one idempotent `End`. `End` is the sole terminal record; there is no parallel producer-finished boolean or terminal-error side channel. It may arrive before outstanding completions without prematurely ending collection. Producer EOF and final admission are one Controller transaction; EOF without a final chunk is a `FinishProducerCommand`. Consequently, concurrent close cannot insert a contradictory boundary between the final accepted operation and producer completion. `ResultPort` retains only unsettled sequence IDs. Dynamic collectors remove consumed result entries, and lazy iterators retain only the bounded out-of-order window rather than a lifetime submission history. A queue publication commits before its sequence/end bookkeeping changes, so an injected local sink failure can be retried without losing the result or publishing a false terminal record. If Pool termination wins before a lazy next admission, the iterator reports one compatibility `PoolTaskError` after already accepted results and then converges to `StopIteration`; it never exposes an internal closed-mailbox error. ## Pool lifecycle ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> RUNNING RUNNING --> CLOSING: CloseCommand RUNNING --> TERMINATING: TerminateCommand RUNNING --> FAILED: fatal Controller error CLOSING --> CLOSED: accepted operations settled and all exits confirmed CLOSING --> TERMINATING: TerminateCommand CLOSING --> FAILED: fatal dispatch or cleanup error TERMINATING --> TERMINATED: results settled and all exits confirmed TERMINATING --> FAILED: bounded cleanup failure CLOSED --> CLOSED: idempotent close or terminate TERMINATED --> TERMINATED: idempotent close or terminate FAILED --> FAILED: idempotent close or terminate ``` Terminal transitions first settle every pending and running operation exactly once, then move every actor-bearing slot to `STOPPING`. Cleanup submission retries use a bounded budget and deadline. Exhaustion preserves the occupied slot and exposes a specific cleanup error; it never reports terminal success or releases capacity without exit proof. `CLOSED`, `TERMINATED`, and `FAILED` are absorbing phases. A terminate that races before graceful close commits still selects `TERMINATING`; once a terminal phase is committed, later close/terminate calls are idempotent and cannot rewrite the original success/failure semantics. In `FAILED`, the Controller continues its already-owned cleanup until every slot is empty or the bounded cleanup error is recorded. Before a terminal Controller exits, it closes command ingress while holding the same short lock used by command senders, then drains commands that linearized earlier. This prevents both lost acknowledgments and commands queued behind a departing Controller. A successfully closed or terminated Controller exits automatically; `join()` does not keep it alive or send a second lifecycle command. ## Class and ownership relationships ```mermaid classDiagram class RayBackend { configure() effective_n_jobs() signature-based Pool capability matching } class Pool { PoolState state Queue control_queue completion registry WeakSet dynamic_result_ports bounded LRU Joblib registries } class PoolController { Queue control_queue Deque pending weak Pool reference run() } class ActorSlotTable { ActorSlot[] slots named transition methods pop_ready() by canonical scan } class ActorSlot { index generation SlotPayload payload } class RunningSlot { actor batch_ref result_port result_sequence } class StopPendingSlot { actor forced stop bookkeeping } class StoppingSlot { ActorTermination termination } class BatchOperation { func batch result_port sequence } class ResultPort { reserve() complete(sequence, outcomes) finish() close(error) cancel() } class ResultThread { consume local ResultPort events preserve sequence order isolate callbacks } RayBackend --> Pool: constructs Pool *-- PoolController Pool *-- ActorSlotTable PoolController --> ActorSlotTable: sole runtime mutator ActorSlotTable *-- ActorSlot ActorSlot *-- RunningSlot ActorSlot *-- StopPendingSlot ActorSlot *-- StoppingSlot PoolController --> BatchOperation: pending deque BatchOperation --> ResultPort RunningSlot --> ResultPort ResultThread --> ResultPort ``` ## Compatibility and bounded resources - Autoscaling remains opt-in; actor resources never change implicitly. - Fixed pools retain eager readiness, completed-batch fairness, crash replacement, callbacks, `imap` timeout behavior, and close/terminate semantics. - Joblib `n_jobs` remains the outer concurrency limit. The Ray backend does not mutate process-global Joblib Pool inheritance. - `maxtasksperchild`, Joblib reuse, NumPy values, Exception-as-data, iterator abandonment, callback failure, serialization failure, actor death, and Ray session errors have direct coverage. - Slot/ref/completion ownership is bounded by `max_size`; Joblib argument caches retain at most `4 * max_size` entries per registry kind. Their oldest-entry eviction is LRU, so a repeatedly shared large input is not discarded merely because it was inserted before ephemeral per-batch values. Dynamic iterator sequence/results bookkeeping is bounded by its active submission window rather than total iterator lifetime. - READY selection is an `O(max_size)` canonical scan. The deliberate small scheduling cost removes a second mutable index. - One isolated daemon `ResultThread` remains per outstanding AsyncResult/iterator to preserve callback and blocking compatibility. The number of caller-created outstanding results and eagerly accepted map operations remains caller-bounded, matching existing Pool behavior. - User code may run forever; shutdown liveness is conditional on Ray resolving the exit Future or the configured hard cleanup deadline producing an explicit failure. The dispatcher deliberately permits only one in-flight batch per actor. This is the property that keeps operation ownership and actor retirement exact, but it adds a public-Future callback and Controller-queue round trip between batches. Local benchmarks show that the cost is visible for `chunksize=1` sub-millisecond work and is increasingly amortized by Joblib batching or longer tasks. Restoring eager actor-mailbox prefetch would improve that case but would reintroduce multiple dispatched-operation owners per slot; bounded prefetch is therefore left as a separate, explicitly modeled design rather than hidden inside this correctness change. ## Suggested review order 1. Control queue linearization and command acknowledgment. 2. `ObjectRef.future()` token ownership and `ActorSlotTable` transitions. 3. `ResultPort` Completion/End counting and lazy-iterator close races. 4. STOPPING ownership, close/terminate/failure convergence, and bounded cleanup. 5. Autoscaling policy and fixed-pool/Joblib compatibility. ## Validation - Complete non-cluster-E2E autoscaling suite: **187 passed, 1 deselected**. - Zero-CPU-head `AutoscalingCluster` E2E: **1 passed**. - Existing multiprocessing and Joblib compatibility suites: **27 passed**. - Explicit compatibility run with Joblib 1.2.0 against the current collected suite: **11 passed**. - Applicable pre-commit hooks: **passed** (ruff, black, pydoclint, semgrep, import order, and repository checks). - `git diff --check` and Python AST/compile checks: **passed**. Commands run in isolated virtual environments against the workspace Python sources and a locally installed Ray wheel: ```bash pytest python/ray/tests/test_joblib_autoscale.py -k 'not test_autoscaling_cluster_e2e' -q pytest python/ray/tests/test_joblib_autoscale.py::test_autoscaling_cluster_e2e -q pytest python/ray/tests/test_multiprocessing.py python/ray/tests/test_joblib.py -q # In the separate Joblib 1.2.0 environment: pytest python/ray/tests/test_joblib.py -q pre-commit run --files python/ray/util/multiprocessing/pool.py python/ray/tests/test_joblib_autoscale.py python -m py_compile python/ray/util/multiprocessing/pool.py python/ray/tests/test_joblib_autoscale.py git diff --check ``` - Deterministic model/fault coverage includes every allowed and forbidden ActorSlot transition; the complete `PoolState × SlotPayload × submit/close/terminate` cross-product; bidirectional slot/ref/completion-owner checks; short command-sequence operation conservation; Future completion before registration; duplicate and stale completion tokens; Future creation and callback-registration failure; atomic eager-map admission; SubmitMany/FinishProducer conservation; command-reply and local result-sink failure; terminal queue draining; End-before-Completion; both previously confirmed `imap`/close races; mixed startup-round success and failure; actor startup, death, retirement, forced exit, stop-submission retry, and exit deadline; Exception-as-data; callback failure; result serialization failure; concurrent submit/close/terminate/join; bounded cleanup retries, LRU registries, and long-lived iterator bookkeeping; fixed pools; repeated scale cycles; Joblib reuse; `maxtasksperchild`; and abandoned iterators. ### Scheduling microbenchmark A repeated local benchmark compared `origin/master`, this branch before the current refactor, and the current workspace. It records whole-map latency/throughput plus the same-actor gap between one batch finishing and the next starting. The 64-actor cases oversubscribe this 8-core host and are retained only as stress evidence; the table below uses the stable 1/8-actor cases. | workload | origin/master | branch before refactor | current | current vs prior branch | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 actor, 0 ms, batch 1 | 2613 tasks/s | 576 tasks/s | 735 tasks/s | +27.6% | | 8 actors, 0 ms, batch 1 | 3601 tasks/s | 1534 tasks/s | 1737 tasks/s | +13.2% | | 1 actor, 0 ms, batch 16 | 11767 tasks/s | 5981 tasks/s | 8771 tasks/s | +46.6% | | 8 actors, 0 ms, batch 16 | 25544 tasks/s | 14296 tasks/s | 18540 tasks/s | +29.7% | | 8 actors, 1 ms, batch 16 | 3203 tasks/s | 2854 tasks/s | 2978 tasks/s | +4.3% | The current refactor improves every listed branch baseline, but does not claim parity with `origin/master` for tiny batches. `origin/master` eagerly fills actor mailboxes and therefore lacks the one-operation-per-actor backpressure/retirement invariant. The measured same-actor median gap for 0 ms, batch 1 is 1.33 ms current versus 0.30 ms on `origin/master` (one actor), and 4.56 ms versus 1.59 ms (eight actors). This is an explicit performance/complexity tradeoff for maintainer review, not an unmeasured assertion. The reviewed branch is pushed at `af3ac33ca9`; all **36 review threads are resolved**. At push time DCO and release passed, while microcheck and Read the Docs were rerunning for this head. The preceding `0509c62f6a` run had an unrelated `test_task_events_2.py::test_fault_tolerance_job_failed[default]` task-reporting duplication (expected 7 tasks, observed 14) and an external PyTorch intersphinx inventory failure. Those preceding-head failures neither validate nor disprove this Pool architecture; the checks for `af3ac33ca9` are authoritative. ## Duplicate-work check Open issues and PRs were checked before development. #31128 is the existing request; no competing implementation was found. #64959 is a duplicate design tracker created during development. ## AI assistance and human accountability AI assistance was used to develop and test this change. - [ ] The human submitter has reviewed every changed line and can defend the final design and implementation. - [ ] The human submitter has independently confirmed the final test results before requesting maintainer review. This PR remains a draft until both items are complete.

signal.title: [Data] Expose read-task resource args in read_webdataset
signal.text: ## Description `read_webdataset` does not allow num_cpus, num_gpus, memory, or ray_remote_args, so users must drop to `read_datasource` and build `WebDatasetDatasource` directly to tune read task resources, while readers of other formats already expose these. This allows users to pass these arguments to `read_webdataset` for consistency and user convenience, which matters when the read is I/O bound. In this case, lowering num_cpus runs more concurrent read tasks for higher S3 throughput. ## Related issues Related to #65394

signal.title: [serve.llm] Skip streaming TPOT jitter test on ARM
signal.text: ## Why are these changes needed? `test_stable_streaming_tpot` checks that disabling stream batching does not add jitter by comparing the server TPOT mean and standard deviation with the direct engine. Shared ARM CI workers introduce enough unrelated scheduling variance to make the standard-deviation assertion flaky. This keeps the original jitter checks on other architectures and skips the test on ARM64. ## Related issue number No open issue or PR duplicates this change. signal.title: [ci] Preinstall cython in the docbuild image
signal.text: ## Description The two doc API check steps (`lint.sh api_annotations` and `api_policy_check`, `job_env: docbuild-py3.11`) pip-install Ray from the checkout at runtime. setup.py declares `setup_requires=["cython >= 3.0.12", ...]`, nothing in the docbuild image satisfies it (the docbuild depset lock carries no cython at all), so setuptools `fetch_build_eggs` spawns an inner pip against the configured index on every run. Since #65578 (armed by #65605), the docbuild image inherits a baked `ENV PIP_INDEX_URL=http://rayci.localhost:35999/simple` from the image roots. Containers started via `ci/ray_ci/linux_container.py` recreate the `--add-host rayci.localhost:host-gateway` mapping, but `job_env` steps launched by the plain docker-buildkite-plugin do not — so the inner pip fails DNS (`[Errno -5] No address associated with hostname`) and both steps fail deterministically, e.g. premerge 72248: ``` ERROR: Could not find a version that satisfies the requirement cython>=3.0.12 (from versions: none) ``` Preinstalling a satisfying cython via the docbuild depset makes `fetch_build_eggs` a no-op: the steps stop needing an index at runtime entirely, which a lint step never should have. This is deliberately the image-side hardening; the structural fix (rayci emitting the host mapping for plugin-run steps, mirroring `linux_container.py`) is tracked separately. ## Changes - `doc/requirements-doc.txt`: pin `cython==3.0.12` (setup.py's floor) — source of truth per the docs lockfile policy. - `python/deplocks/docs/docbuild_depset_py3.11.lock`: regenerated, gains only the cython block. ## Verification - Lock regenerated with `bazelisk run //ci/raydepsets:raydepsets -- build ci/raydepsets/configs/docs.depsets.yaml --name docbuild_depset_311`; diff is the single cython entry. - CI's `raydepsets --check` enforces source/lock consistency; the rebuilt docbuild image (lock is in wanda `srcs`) will run both API check steps in this PR. Not a duplicate: no open PR touches the docbuild depset or these steps' cython handling. AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to triage the failure and prepare this PR. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signal.title: [ci][doc] Log builder CPU and memory around the RtD Sphinx build
signal.text: ## Summary Read the Docs builds intermittently fail with a bare `EOFError` raised from `multiprocessing/connection.py`, with no document named and no cause given: ``` Traceback ========= File ".../multiprocessing/connection.py", line 399, in _recv raise EOFError EOFError make: *** [Makefile:91: html] Error 2 ``` `doc/Makefile` builds with `-j auto`, so Sphinx forks one write worker per CPU. When a worker dies, the parent reports only that `EOFError`. This PR wraps the existing `make` invocation in the `.readthedocs.yaml` html job so the builder's CPU count, cgroup memory ceiling, peak memory, and cgroup OOM counters print around every build. It's a measurement step, not a fix. Nothing about the build changes. ## Why this isn't a content problem - The point in the write phase where it surfaces moves between builds: 58%, 78%, and 92% across three recent failures. A bad document would fail at the same place every time. - Five builds in the last two days failed with this signature, one of them on `master`. Every other RtD failure in that window is an ordinary `fail_on_warning` trip. - One PR hit it after passing an hour earlier on the same base commit, and other PRs built successfully in the same window. | Build | When (UTC) | Version | Died at | |---|---|---|---| | 4343286 | Aug 20 21:52 | PR preview | 58% | | 4343129 | Aug 20 21:11 | PR preview | 92% | | 4343048 | Aug 20 20:59 | PR preview | — | | 4342961 | Aug 20 20:35 | PR preview | — | | 4339216 | Aug 20 03:41 | `master` | 78% | ## Why measure before capping `-j` The likely mechanism is the kernel OOM-killing a write worker. Lowering `-j` is the obvious response, but choosing a value blind would cost wall-clock on every doc build and might buy nothing, since the useful cap depends on how many CPUs the builder actually has. If the builder has two CPUs, `-j auto` is already 2 and a cap isn't the answer at all. The cgroup `memory.events` OOM counters settle whether an OOM kill is even what's happening. ## Implementation notes - The diagnostics run around the build rather than in a `post_build` job because `post_build` is skipped when the build fails, and the failing build is the one worth measuring. - `rc` carries `make`'s exit status through to the job's exit, so a real Sphinx failure still fails the build. Verified under `sh -e` that the diagnostics run and the non-zero status propagates. - Every probe is guarded with `|| true` or `|| echo`, so a missing file or a non-matching `grep` can't abort the job under `set -e`. - The script avoids the constructs the RtD job runner is known to mishandle, per the existing comments in this file: no `printf` with escape sequences, no backslash escapes, and no shell comments inside the block. - Validated with `sh -n` and by parsing the YAML. ## Follow-up Once a few builds have reported their numbers, this wrapper comes back out along with whatever the real fix turns out to be.

signal.title: [ci] Give whl_library a pip that can read a JSON index
signal.text: ## What Declares `pypi__pip` at **pip 23.3.2** in `WORKSPACE`, ahead of the one `rules_python` brings, so the pip `whl_library` shells out to can read a PEP 691 JSON simple index. ## Why An index page served as JSON is skipped rather than parsed, and the resolve then fails as though the package did not exist: ``` Skipping page .../simple/pygments/ because the GET request got Content-Type: application/vnd.pypi.simple.v1+json. The only supported Content-Type is text/html ERROR: Could not find a version that satisfies the requirement pygments==2.16.1 (from versions: none) ``` `rules_python` arrives transitively — protobuf's `protobuf_deps()` pins it at **0.14.0** — and 0.14.0 bundles **pip 22.2.1**, one release before JSON support landed in 22.3. The error wording is itself the version tell: pip phrases it that way only while it lacks PEP 691. This matters for the CI mirror. It caches an index page keyed on URL while PyPI answers `Vary: Accept`, so whichever client warms an entry fixes the representation for every later reader — uv asks for JSON, this pip can only read HTML. `ci/pypi_index_proxy.py` pins the upstream request to HTML for exactly that reason (#65593), but pinning producers only holds while every producer cooperates, and it cannot evict an entry already stored. **A pip that reads JSON reads HTML too**, so moving this one forward makes the representation stop mattering in either direction, which is a property rather than a convention. ## Why override one wheel instead of bumping rules_python `pip_install_dependencies()` declares its deps through `maybe()`, which skips any repository that already exists — so declaring `pypi__pip` earlier wins, and the blast radius is the single pip bazel shells out to for python dependency extraction. A `rules_python` bump would be a migration, not a bump: this WORKSPACE uses `pip_install_dependencies`, the `interpreter` symbol from `@python3_10`, and `pip_parse` attributes that all changed after 0.14.0, and newer `rules_python` drops the WORKSPACE mode this build runs in (bazel 7.5.0, `--noenable_bzlmod`). 23.3.2 rather than the newest release: comfortably past 22.3, without pairing a 2022-era `whl_library` with a much later pip CLI. ## Testing ``` $ bazel fetch @pypi__pip//:lib INFO: Analyzed target @@pypi__pip//:lib (7 packages loaded, 537 targets configured). INFO: All external dependencies for the requested targets fetched successfully. $ ls $(bazel info output_base)/external/pypi__pip BUILD.bazel WORKSPACE pip pip-23.3.2.dist-info $ grep ^__version__ $(bazel info output_base)/external/pypi__pip/pip/__init__.py __version__ = "23.3.2" ``` So the override takes precedence over rules_python's 22.2.1 and the generated build file resolves. `buildifier --mode=check WORKSPACE` clean. Wheel URL and sha256 come from the PyPI JSON API for 23.3.2. Observed downstream in rayturbo build 14076 (`pygments==2.16.1`) and fixed there by the same change, anyscale/rayturbo#4217. Not a duplicate: no open PR touches `pypi__pip` or the `rules_python` pin — #65538 and #65567 are unrelated CI work. AI assistance was used for this change.
signal.author: elliot-barn

signal.title: [Feat][Core/Auth] Enable token authentication for local clusters by default
signal.text: ## Description Enable token authentication for local clusters by default. The table below shows the resulting behavior. Remote and worker paths are unchanged. | Entry point | `RAY_AUTH_MODE` unset, token exists | `RAY_AUTH_MODE` unset, no token | `RAY_AUTH_MODE=token` | `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` | |---|---|---|---|---| | **`ray.init()`** (new local cluster, no address) | enable + **reuse** token | enable + **generate** token | enable (generate/reuse) | disabled, no warning | | **`ray start --head`** (local head) | enable + reuse token | disabled + **warn** | enable; **raises** if no token | disabled + **warn** | | **`ray.init(address=…)`** (connect to existing) | unchanged, no auto-enable; needs token if cluster requires it | unchanged | requires token, else error | disabled | | **`ray start --address=…`** (worker) | unchanged, no auto-enable | unchanged | requires token, else error | disabled | A token "exists" if any of these resolve, checked in order: 1. `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN` environment variable 2. file at `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH` 3. default file `~/.ray/auth_token` ## Related issues N/A ## Additional information To enable this for all clusters in the future: - Change the default to "token" here: https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/1439e47b9b136143fbc99417cb4f50a82eff72a9/src/ray/common/ray_config_def.h#L39. That is the single source of truth, and `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` stays as the opt-out. - Remove the auto-enable helper functions from this PR (`enable_token_auth_by_default`, `maybe_enable_token_auth_if_token_available`) and their call sites in `worker.py` and `scripts.py`. - Decide whether `ray start --head` should auto-generate a token instead of erroring. The worker and connect paths would then require a distributed token, which is a breaking change. - The cluster launcher, KubeRay, and autoscaler would need to distribute the token to workers automatically. Test fixtures would need to provision a token, and every client path would need to attach it. - Update `token-auth.md` and the guides that say "disabled by default".

signal.title: [llm][ci] Upgrade to vllm 0.27.0
signal.text: ## Description Upgrades vLLM 0.26.0 -> 0.27.0. vLLM 0.27.0 re-parents request errors onto `VLLMError` instead of `ValueError`, turning ordinary bad requests into 500s: - pydantic no longer wraps them during request parsing, so the ingress never sees a `ValidationError`. We added an explicit 4xx mapping in this PR. - `AsyncLLM.generate` re-raises only `VLLMClientError` and wraps everything else in `EngineGenerateError`, erasing the 4xx type. We added a temporary unwrap and will remove once vllm-project/vllm#52394 lands. vLLM 0.27.0 defaults to DeepEP V2 which needs `nccl >= 2.30.4` (`nccl_overrides.txt`), and the `sglang` release image now uninstalls `flashinfer` first, since 0.27 bumps it to `0.6.16.post3` while `sglang` pins `0.6.12`. ## Deferred Multimodal chat under KV-aware token forwarding. Since vllm-project/vllm#48145 the renderer builds engine input from the forwarded ids and skips chat rendering, which drops `multi_modal_data`. Left a TODO in code, and I'll address it in a follow-up while enabling multimodality support for `KVAwareRouter`. ## Related issues > Link related issues: "Fixes #1234", "Closes #1234", or "Related to #1234". ## Additional information > Optional: Add implementation details, API changes, usage examples, screenshots, etc.

signal.title: [TPU] Add PyTorch TPU environment variable and runtime_env APIs to Slice and Subslice placement groups
signal.text: ## What do these changes do? This PR introduces APIs to generate PyTorch TPU environment variables (`TORCH_TPU_TOPOLOGY` and `TORCH_TPU_SLICEBUILDER_ADDRESSES`) for TPU pod slices and multi-host sub-slices. ### Key Changes * **`ray.util.tpu.get_torchtpu_env_vars`**: Added a standalone helper to compute `TORCH_TPU_TOPOLOGY` and `TORCH_TPU_SLICEBUILDER_ADDRESSES`, handling 3D (`v4`, `v5p`, `v5litepod`, `v6e`) and 4D (`v7x` dual-chiplet) topology string normalization. * **`SlicePlacementGroup` & `SubslicePlacementGroup` APIs**: Added `.get_tpu_env_vars()` and `.get_tpu_runtime_env()` methods. These two methods currently only set PyTorch related vars, but could be extended in the future as necessary. From my testing I did not find it necessary to set any additional libtpu/XLA env vars for Torch or JAX workloads to work. * `SlicePlacementGroup`: Delegates to `get_torchtpu_env_vars()` for full pod slice topologies. * `SubslicePlacementGroup`: Partitions parent slicebuilder endpoints (`TORCH_TPU_SLICEBUILDER_ADDRESSES`) across multi-host sub-slices using worker ID label selectors (`RAY_NODE_TPU_WORKER_ID_KEY`) to map the address to the correct ID, with fallback to a remote task querying bundle index `0` for the env var when unset locally. * Added `get_tpu_cores_per_chip` and `get_tpu_resource_per_chip` helpers in `ray._private.accelerators.tpu` ## Related issue number https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/64055 ## How was this tested? - [x] Unit Tests - [x] Manual tests - process in comments

signal.title: [core] feat(rdt): enable driver-side ray.put with NIXL tensor transport
signal.text: Allow ray.put(value, _tensor_transport='nixl') from a driver process. Previously this failed because get_runtime_context().current_actor raises RuntimeError in a non-actor context. Changes: - Make RDTMeta.src_actor and TransferMetadata.src_actor Optional - Catch RuntimeError in put_object and set src_actor=None for driver - Reject two-sided transports (NCCL/GLOO) from driver with clear error - Guard src_actor dereferences in _abort_transport and transfer paths - Handle free_object_primary_copy locally for driver-owned objects - Raise ValueError for _use_object_store=True on driver-owned RDT objects - Align worker.py error to RuntimeError with 'one-sided transport' message Fixes ray-project/ray#64714 ## Tests Three new tests in `python/ray/tests/rdt/test_rdt_nixl.py`: ### `test_driver_put_nixl` End-to-end driver-side NIXL flow: 1. `ray.put(tensor, _tensor_transport="nixl")` from the driver 2. Verify `src_actor is None` in RDT metadata 3. Verify tensor registered in NIXL transport 4. Actor consumes the driver-created ref via `actor.sum.remote(ref)` 5. Driver-local `ray.get(ref)` returns the original tensor 6. After `del ref` + `gc.collect()`, verify cleanup: tensor freed, RDT metadata removed, NIXL metadata removed, tensor descriptor cache cleared ### `test_driver_owned_rdt_rejects_object_store_fallback` Verify `_use_object_store=True` on a driver-owned RDT object raises `ValueError` matching `_use_object_store=True` instead of crashing with `AttributeError` on `None.__ray_call__`. ### `test_driver_rejects_two_sided_transport` Verify `ray.put(tensor, _tensor_transport="nccl")` from the driver raises `RuntimeError` matching `one-sided transport`. Two-sided transports require an actor context to coordinate the send. ### Running ```bash # New driver tests pytest -sv python/ray/tests/rdt/test_rdt_nixl.py \ -k "test_driver_put_nixl or test_driver_rejects_two_sided_transport or test_driver_owned_rdt_rejects_object_store_fallback" ``` ### Results | Test | Result | |------|--------| | `test_driver_put_nixl` | PASSED | | `test_driver_owned_rdt_rejects_object_store_fallback` | PASSED | | `test_driver_rejects_two_sided_transport` | PASSED |
