signal.title: [Data] Expose which backpressure policy is blocking an operator in execution diagnostics
signal.text: ### Description Ray Data currently applies multiple independent `BackpressurePolicy` implementations (e.g. concurrency cap, resource budget, downstream capacity) when deciding whether an operator can accept more input. When an operator is blocked, the progress bar already shows a `[backpressure]` label, and `ds.stats()` reports per-operator timing/memory stats — but neither surfaces which policy caused the block, so all backpressure cases look identical from the outside. The scheduling loop already evaluates policies in order and knows which one returned `False` for `can_add_input(op)`. A minimal change would: 1. Record the triggered policy's name when an operator is blocked. 2. Expose it as part of existing operator stats, e.g. appended to the `stats()` output: ``` Operator 2 MapBatches(Inference): 4 tasks executed, 12 blocks produced in 5.1s * Backpressured: True (reason: DownstreamCapacityBackpressurePolicy) ... ``` 3. Optionally include it in the progress bar tooltip/label instead of the generic `[backpressure]` text. This doesn't change scheduling behavior or add a new policy — just makes an existing internal decision observable, and would fit naturally into the existing stats/diagnostics model. ### Use case When an operator in a Ray Data pipeline shows [backpressure] in the progress bar or has a growing input queue, it's unclear why — whether it's the concurrency cap, insufficient resource budget, or downstream capacity. Each cause needs a different fix (raise concurrency, free up cluster resources, or scale the downstream operator instead), so without knowing the actual cause, users often tune the wrong parameter and waste a debugging cycle. Currently the only way to find out is to read executor logs and manually trace which BackpressurePolicy.can_add_input() call returned False. This is especially painful in pipelines with several chained map_batches / actor-pool stages, where it's often not obvious which stage is the actual bottleneck.
signal.author: mimosapudical

signal.title: [serve] Add separate fast path for unary gRPC direct ingress
signal.text: ## What Currently, a unary request returns its single response through an interposed async generator instead of returning directly. Instead we split the handler into three pieces to maintain the speed of the unary-unary hot path. 1. `_prepare_direct_ingress_grpc_request` does the setup every request needs regardless of shape. 2. `_direct_ingress_grpc_unary_response` handles calls that return exactly one response. Returns the response directly. 3. `_direct_ingress_grpc_streaming_response` stays a generator and handles calls that yield a stream. Setup and teardown still are shared. The only difference is how they consume the response. ## Why Unary gRPC throughput on `pytest_serve_throughput_optimized_microbenchmarks` dropped when the handlers were unified, and this recovers most of it. Numbers are average rps from the release test. | metric | before | now | with this change | |---|---:|---:|---:| | `grpc_avg_rps` | 4710.6 | 4601.1 | 4684.1 | | `grpc_100_max_ongoing_requests_avg_rps` | 4726.2 | 4641.3 | 4678.3 | | `grpc_800_max_ongoing_requests_avg_rps` | 4759.7 | 4675.7 | 4731.0 |

signal.title: [serve] Deflake test_cluster on loaded CI shards
signal.text: ## Why `test_cluster` is the tightest-budgeted serve target on the shared Windows shard: 2 FLAKY / 0 FAILED in 23 runs, max observed runtime **238s against the 300s limit** implied by `size = "medium"` — 79% of budget. The `linux` target from the same block is slightly worse at **241.5s (80.5%)**. The shard has zero hard failures across its 19 tracked tests, which points at timeout and slow convergence rather than assertion bugs. `test_cluster` also co-flaked with `test_proxy` on postmerge build 19184. For comparison on the same shard: `test_grpc` is `enormous` (45% used), `test_standalone` `enormous` (21%), `test_per_request_headers` `large` + `timeout="eternal"` (28%), `test_metrics` `medium` + `timeout="long"` (60%). ## What **1. Bazel headroom.** `test_cluster.py` moves into its own `py_test_module_list` with `timeout = "long"` (300s → 900s). The block carries no `no_windows` tag, so this covers both the `windows` and `linux` targets. Only the shared-medium entry moves; the `no_windows` pack-scheduling variant is left alone. **2. Load-sensitivity fixes in the test itself.** - 22 `wait_for_condition` calls were on the bare 10s default. All now take one `WAIT_TIMEOUT_S = 60` module constant, which is also reused as the `get_pids` collection budget (previously a separate hardcoded 30). Five hand-picked sub-budgets (`timeout=15/25/30`) collapse into the same constant. - Two `list_actors` calls omitted `filters=[("STATE", "=", "ALIVE")]`, so they counted DEAD actors and an exact-count wait could never recover once an actor restarted. The comment above one of them already read "Total alive actors", so this restores the documented intent. - Two `client._wait_for_application_running("default")` calls relied on the default `timeout_s=-1`. The loop guard is `while ... < timeout_s or timeout_s < 0`, so that branch is permanently true and the `else: raise TimeoutError` is unreachable — the call cannot time out. Under contention the test hung until pytest-timeout killed it at 600s, burning the whole budget with no useful diagnostic. Both are now bounded. The two `timeout_s=1` calls are deliberately untouched: they sit inside `pytest.raises(TimeoutError)` and assert a replica has *not* started yet. ## Validation Interleaved A/B on a 4-CPU box under synthetic CPU load, 3 reps × (baseline, patched), arms alternating so external drift hits both equally:
signal.author: johntaylor-cell

signal.title: [serve] Deflake test_grpc - drop the redundant ray_shutdown fixture
signal.text: All 23 fixture-using tests in test_grpc.py take both ray_instance and ray_shutdown, and the two undo each other. ray_shutdown's setup body runs serve.shutdown() + ray.shutdown(), tearing down the cluster ray_instance just created; that serve.shutdown() runs with Ray down so it reaches _connect(), which re-inits Ray just to look for a controller. The test body then starts with Ray uninitialized and serve.start() implicitly creates a third, default cluster - without the _metrics_export_port / _system_config that ray_instance exists to supply. So each of these tests starts three Ray clusters instead of one and silently discards its fixture configuration. Each extra startup is another chance to lose a cluster-startup race, which fits this target being the flakiest Serve target on Windows (~17% of runs vs ~2.6% on Linux, always green on retry). ray_instance already does serve.shutdown() + ray.shutdown() in its own teardown, so ray_shutdown is pure overhead wherever ray_instance is present. Tests that use ray_shutdown on its own are correct and are left alone. Measured on an empty test, counting Ray session dirs: 3 clusters / 32s with both fixtures vs 1 cluster / 12s with ray_instance alone. On four real tests from this file, both arms green: 12 clusters / 145.9s before, 4 / 68.7s after.
signal.author: johntaylor-cell

signal.title: [serve] Deflake test_proxy on loaded CI shards
signal.text: test_proxy flakes 14% of postmerge runs on the Windows serve shard (3 flaky, 0 hard failures in 22 runs). It is load-sensitive in three ways: - The bazel target was `size = "medium"` with no explicit timeout, so a 300s limit against a 194s max observed runtime -- 65% of budget, the tightest of any serve target on that shard bar test_cluster. Every comparable target there already carries an explicit `long`/`eternal` or is `enormous`. Give it `timeout = "long"`. - 9 of 11 wait_for_condition calls ran on the bare 10s default while waiting on three-node cluster convergence and proxy HEALTHY/DRAINING/DRAINED transitions. Route them through a named WAIT_TIMEOUT_S. - One request_with_retries used timeout=1.0, which is both the httpx timeout and the outer retry budget, so it got a single attempt on a busy box. Also filter three list_actors() calls to STATE = ALIVE. They back exact-count waits, and counting DEAD actors means the count never recovers once anything restarts. A fourth site in the same test already filtered, so the file was internally inconsistent. No assertions change.

signal.title: fix(serve): return 404 status code when application or deployment not found (#51442)
signal.text: ## Description Makes the Serve dashboard scale endpoint report client errors with 404 status code instead of 400 when an application or deployment is not found. #51417 added the `HTTPStatusCode` enum and the `rest_response(status_code=...)` plumbing, but adoption across dashboard modules is ongoing. **Backend (`python/ray/dashboard/modules/serve/serve_head.py`):** - In `scale_deployment`, when `ValueError` with `"not found"` occurred (looking up a nonexistent application or deployment), the endpoint returned HTTP 400 (Bad Request). Scaling a nonexistent resource is a client error representing a missing resource, so it now returns HTTP 404 (Not Found). ## Related issues Related to #51442 (umbrella: revisit Ray dashboard API status codes). Since #51442 is an umbrella issue, this PR covers the `serve_head.py` scope only, allowing each dashboard module to be reviewed independently. ## Tests Updated the existing unit test `test_error_case` in `python/ray/dashboard/modules/serve/tests/test_serve_dashboard.py`: - Verified that scaling a nonexistent application (`app_name="nonexistent"`) returns HTTP status code 404 instead of 400. ## Not a duplicate Checked existing open issues and PRs for #51442. No active PR currently addresses status code fixes for `serve_head.py`. Commented on #51442 prior to working on this scope.
signal.author: CrossManger

signal.title: [core] Guarantee each pending lease request only receives at most one CancelWorkerLease RPC
signal.text: In #65420 we made changes to reduce the number of duplicate CancelWorkerLease RPCs sent to pending leases on a raylet, specifically targeting the message reordering case. However, there's still a potential gap where in the current lease code, when the number of submitted tasks drops to 0 for a certain scheduling key, we'll attempt to cancel any pending leases. This makes sense, but in the case where a lease request takes a long time to reply (say a transient network failure), we could potentially spam multiple CancelWorkerLease RPCs for the same lease. Every single time the number of submitted tasks drops to 0 we spray CancelWorkerLease RPCs for all pending leases, so potentially we could have this number fluctuate from 0 -> 1 -> 0 -> 1 ... and every time it hits 0 thats one more CancelWorkerLease RPC queued up. This PR patches that up, so that we now can guarantee that for every unique lease request, we only send at most one CancelWorkerLease RPC. Added a unit test to verify this change.
signal.author: Sparks0219

signal.title: [Data] write_lance is incompatible with PyLance 6.x due to removed storage_options_provider argument
signal.text: ### What happened + What you expected to happen ## Description Ray 2.55.1 passes the keyword argument `storage_options_provider` to PyLance write APIs, but PyLance removed that argument https://github.com/lance-format/lance/pull/6186 and replaced it with `namespace_client` / `table_id`. As a result `Dataset.write_lance()` fails with newer versions of lance: ```text TypeError: write_fragments() got an unexpected keyword argument 'storage_options_provider' ``` ## Reproduction ```python import ray ds = ray.data.from_items([{"id": 1, "text": "a"}, {"id": 2, "text": "b"}]) ds.write_lance("/tmp/ray-lance-test") ``` Actual: ```text ray.exceptions.RayTaskError(TypeError): ray::Write() TypeError: write_fragments() got an unexpected keyword argument 'storage_options_provider' ``` Expected: the dataset is written, or Ray fails fast with a clear version-compatibility error. ## Root cause In `/ray/data/_internal/datasource/lance_datasink.py` the argument is passed unconditionally, even when no namespace is configured and the provider is `None` (lines 130-150): ```python storage_options_provider = create_storage_options_provider( namespace_impl, namespace_properties, table_id ) write_fragments( reader, uri, ..., storage_options=storage_options, storage_options_provider=storage_options_provider, ) ``` Three call sites are affected, so fixing only `write_fragments()` would leave the append and commit paths broken: | Line | Call | | --- | --- | | 149 | `write_fragments(..., storage_options_provider=...)` | | 250 | `lance.LanceDataset(..., storage_options_provider=...)` (APPEND) | | 306 | `lance.LanceDataset.commit(..., storage_options_provider=...)` | All three PyLance targets dropped the parameter in 6.x: | PyLance 6.0.1 API | `storage_options_provider` | `namespace_client` | | --- | --- | --- | | `write_fragments` | absent | present | | `LanceDataset.__init__` | absent | present | | `LanceDataset.commit` | absent | present | ## Affected versions Inspected the Python / `.pyi` sources of each published wheel: | PyLance | `storage_options_provider` | | --- | --- | | 6.0.0 – 9.0.0 (latest) | **absent** | ## Suggested fix Support the current PyLance API by selecting `storage_options_provider` vs `namespace_client` / `table_id` based on the installed signature at all three call sites, and omit the namespace argument entirely for plain URI writes. ### Versions / Dependencies ray==2.55.1 pylance==6.0.1 ### Reproduction script ```python import ray ds = ray.data.from_items([{"id": 1, "text": "a"}, {"id": 2, "text": "b"}]) ds.write_lance("/tmp/ray-lance-test") ``` ### Issue Severity Low: It annoys or frustrates me.

signal.title: [core][autoscaler][v1] Skip DEAD GCS nodes in LoadMetrics so they can not overwrite a live node's idle state by IP
signal.text: Autoscaler v1 can fail to terminate an idle worker if GCS returned two NodeStates for the same IP: a live IDLE row with idle_duration_ms > 0, and a DEAD row with idle unset (0). This can happen when an IP is reused by a new node. The LoadMetrics in Autoscaler v1 are keyed by IP, and last write wins, so the DEAD record with idle unset (0) stored last_used = now, and then the node with the same IP no longer looked idle, thus not being terminated. This PR fixes this by skipping DEAD rows in LoadMetrics.

signal.title: [docs] Style pass on the Ray Sandboxes networking section
signal.text: ## Description Style-only follow-up on the "Networking and DNS" section added in #65570. No technical claim changes, and the section's structure and content are the author's; this is polish against the [Ray documentation style guide](https://docs.ray.io/en/master/ray-contribute/writing-style.html). I was asked for a docs review on #65570 but it merged before I finished, so the feedback is landing here instead of as suggestions on a merged PR. ### What changed The one pattern worth naming, because it repeats: the new prose was hard-wrapped at roughly 72 columns while the rest of the page uses one source line per paragraph. The guide asks for [soft-wrapped prose](https://docs.ray.io/en/master/ray-contribute/writing-style.html#soft-wrap-prose) so diffs stay legible. Beyond that: * **Sentence splits** where an em dash, a semicolon, or a mid-sentence colon was joining clauses. The guide asks us to [restructure rather than punctuate](https://docs.ray.io/en/master/ray-contribute/writing-style.html#sentence-structure). After this the whole page is free of Unicode dashes. * **`### DNS in locked-down networks`** instead of a bold paragraph lead-in. The guide reserves [bold](https://docs.ray.io/en/master/ray-contribute/writing-style.html#bold-and-italics) for UI elements, admonition lead-ins, and definition lists. As a real heading it also picks up a TOC entry and a linkable anchor. A `note` admonition would work too if you'd rather it read as an aside. * **Dropped `— **recommended for internet access**`** from the `public` row's first cell. That's bold for emphasis, and the prose above the table already makes the recommendation. * **Parallel structure in the `_oci_spec_transform_fn` list.** The second bullet had lost the `**Term**: explanation` shape of the first and grown to four sentences, so the migration guidance moves into prose after the list. This also drops "no longer need this hook," which orients a reader who knew the previous behavior rather than one arriving fresh. * **A complete lead-in** above the `network="public"` example, which was a noun phrase with a colon on the end. * **Direct advice and active voice**: "Prefer `public` for untrusted code" to "Use `public`", and "Anything beyond that can be configured" to "Configure anything beyond that." ### One question I couldn't answer myself The `sandbox` row's "Network access" cell reads "gVisor netstack," which says how the mode is implemented but not what the reader gets. Does `network="sandbox"` provide egress, or is it isolated like `none`? That's what someone scanning the table to pick a mode is asking, and it's the one cell that doesn't answer it. I left the cell alone rather than guess. Happy to add a few words here if you tell me which it is. ## Related issues Follows #65570. Related to #64964. ## Additional information `DOCKER_DEFAULT_CAPABILITIES` is in the sandbox package's `__all__`, so naming it in the prose above the example is safe. `myst_heading_anchors = 4`, so the new H3 and the existing `#pass-custom-oci-configurations-to-gvisor` link both resolve. Note that no pre-commit hook covers Markdown under `doc/source/`, and Vale is scoped to the Ray Data docs and the example gallery, so nothing lints this file automatically. Verified by hand: heading depth tops out at H3, no stacked headings, and both in-page anchors match real headings.

signal.title: [docs] Replace Unicode punctuation inside copyable code blocks with ASCII
signal.text: ## Summary Replaces Unicode punctuation inside copyable code blocks with plain ASCII, across five doc pages. Readers copy code blocks into a shell or an editor. A smart quote that looks like a string delimiter, or an en dash that looks like a hyphen, is a syntax error waiting to happen and a confusing one to debug, because the character renders almost identically to the ASCII form it isn't. `rllib-advanced-api.rst` is the clearest case. A class path wrapped in curly double quotes sits two lines above the real `"type": "EpsilonGreedy"` entry it describes: ```python # Exploration sub-class by name or full path to module+class # (e.g., "ray.rllib.utils.exploration.epsilon_greedy.EpsilonGreedy") "type": "EpsilonGreedy", ``` Anyone copying the commented form as a starting point gets an invalid literal. ## What changed | File | Fix | |---|---| | `rllib/rllib-advanced-api.rst` | Curly double quotes to straight, around a class path in a Python comment | | `data/saving-data.rst` | Curly apostrophe to none (reworded); box-drawing comment banner to a plain comment | | `train/user-guides/asynchronous-validation.rst` | Em dash to a sentence break, in a Python comment | | `train/user-guides/data-loading-preprocessing.rst` | Same, in the parallel snippet | | `ray-contribute/dependency-management.md` | Em dash to a sentence break, in a Bash comment | ## What deliberately stayed Scope is punctuation inside code blocks that has a plain ASCII equivalent. Prose is untouched, since em dashes read fine there and Ray's style guide doesn't ban them. Captured program output stayed as-is even inside code blocks, because it's a reproduction rather than something to copy and run: - Box-drawing table borders in `testoutput` blocks in `data/saving-data.rst`, `data/quickstart.rst`, and `ray-contribute/writing-code-snippets.md`. These are compared against real output, so changing them breaks the doctest. - Progress-bar labels using a single-character ellipsis in `serve/tutorials/aws-neuron-core-inference.md`. - Directory-tree diagrams in `serve/tutorials/triton-server-integration.md`, which use non-breaking spaces for alignment. - The verbatim GSM8K prompt in `cluster/kubernetes/examples/verl-post-training.md`. Normalizing its apostrophe would misquote the dataset. ## Verification The affected `testcode` blocks parse identically as Python before and after the change, so nothing that ran before stops running. Vale passes on the changed files.

signal.title: [dashboard] Configurable defaults + UI dialogs for py-spy/memray profiling params
signal.text: ## Why are these changes needed? The Ray Dashboard's profiling actions — **Stack Trace** (py-spy), **CPU Flame Graph** (py-spy), and **Memory Profiling** (memray) — expose several parameters (`native`, `subprocesses`, `idle`, `leaks`, `trace_python_allocators`, `duration`, `format`) whose defaults were **hardcoded**. The only way to change one (e.g. to include native C/C++ frames in a stack trace) was to hand-edit the request URL's query string, and there was **no way for a cluster operator to change a default cluster-wide**. This came up from a user asking whether the default value of `native` can be configured — today it can't. This PR makes every profiling parameter's default configurable and gives the dashboard UI first-class controls for them. ### Backend - New `RAY_DASHBOARD_PROFILING_*` environment variables, read on the Ray head node, let an operator set each default. Parse sites in `reporter_head` fall back to these constants only when the request omits the parameter; an **explicit query parameter still wins**, so behavior is unchanged unless an operator opts in. - `duration` and `format` are split into **CPU** and **memory** variants, because py-spy (CPU: `flamegraph`/`raw`/`speedscope`) and memray (memory: `flamegraph`/`table`) accept **different** valid format sets and different duration defaults (5s vs 10s). A single shared default would break CPU requests. `format` defaults are validated against the correct set at load time, falling back to `flamegraph` on a bad value. - **`duration` validation now returns HTTP 400, not 500.** The endpoints previously raised a bare `ValueError` for an over-long duration, which surfaced as an uncaught HTTP 500. `_query_duration` now raises `aiohttp.web.HTTPBadRequest` for a non-integer or out-of-range value. - **The accepted `duration` range is `[1, RAY_DASHBOARD_PROFILING_MAX_DURATION_S]`**, defaulting to the 60s cap the endpoints have always enforced. Operators raise or lower it per cluster. Configured duration *defaults* are clamped into that range at load time — with a warning naming the offending env var — so a misconfigured head node can never bypass the endpoint cap. - `native` remains **Linux-only** regardless of the default (existing guard in `profile_manager`). - `/api/profiling_enabled` now also returns the configured defaults so the UI can seed its dialogs, including `maxDuration`, so the duration field validates against the real cap instead of a hardcoded one. - The valid format sets live in `ray_constants` and are now read by **both** `reporter_head` (to validate the configured default) and `profile_manager` (to validate the request), so the accepted formats are declared in exactly one place. New env vars, all documented in `profiling.md` (10 total): `RAY_DASHBOARD_PROFILING_NATIVE_DEFAULT`, `_SUBPROCESSES_DEFAULT`, `_IDLE_DEFAULT`, `_LEAKS_DEFAULT`, `_TRACE_PYTHON_ALLOCATORS_DEFAULT`, `_CPU_DURATION_DEFAULT`, `_MEMORY_DURATION_DEFAULT`, `_CPU_FORMAT_DEFAULT`, `_MEMORY_FORMAT_DEFAULT`, `RAY_DASHBOARD_PROFILING_MAX_DURATION_S`. ### Frontend - The **Stack Trace** and **CPU Flame Graph** buttons (worker/actor/node/job and task variants) were bare links that hardcoded `native=0`, which also **overrode** the operator's configured default. They are now parameter dialogs — the same UX as the existing Memory Profiling dialog — so users set parameters in the UI instead of editing URLs. - All three profiling dialogs render one shared `ProfilingParamsDialog` component and seed their initial values from the defaults returned by `/api/profiling_enabled`. The hardcoded `native=0` is gone; format options are profiler-correct; the duration field validates against the backend's reported `maxDuration` and disables submit with an inline error when out of range. ## Not a duplicate Searched open PRs before starting — no PR addresses this area: ``` gh pr list --repo ray-project/ray --state open --search "dashboard profiling native default" # No Pull Requests gh pr list --repo ray-project/ray --state open --search "RAY_DASHBOARD_PROFILING" # No Pull Requests ``` There is no existing mechanism for configuring dashboard profiling defaults; `RAY_DASHBOARD_ENABLE_PROFILING` only gates the feature on/off. ## Related issues <!-- Link the source issue/discussion here if one exists. --> ## Checks AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to author this change; every changed line was reviewed by the submitter. **Backend — verified locally:** ``` pytest python/ray/dashboard/modules/reporter/tests/test_reporter.py \ -k "query or clamp or validated_profiling_format" -v # 30 passed pytest python/ray/dashboard/modules/reporter/tests/test_reporter.py -k "profiling_enabled" -v # 1 passed pytest python/ray/dashboard/modules/reporter/tests/test_profile_manager.py -v # 13 passed ``` Tests in `test_reporter.py`: `test_query_flag`, `test_query_duration_valid`, `test_query_duration_invalid_raises_bad_request`, `test_clamp_profiling_duration`, `test_clamp_profiling_duration_warns_and_names_the_env_var`, `test_clamp_profiling_duration_silent_when_in_range`, `test_validated_profiling_format`, `test_validated_profiling_format_absent_uses_fallback`, `test_profiling_enabled_endpoint_returns_defaults`. These cover that out-of-range durations surface as HTTP 400 rather than a bare `ValueError`, that a misconfigured env default is clamped with a warning, and that the CPU/memory format split rejects `speedscope` for memray and `table` for py-spy. New `TestProfilingFormatValidation` in `test_profile_manager.py` asserts both profilers honor the shared format sets — every declared CPU format reaches the py-spy command, every declared memory format maps to its memray subcommand, and each profiler rejects the other's formats. It mocks out subprocess execution, so unlike the live `TestMemoryProfiling` suite it also runs on macOS. End-to-end against a live head node (`RAY_DASHBOARD_ENABLE_PROFILING=1`): ``` GET /api/profiling_enabled -> maxDuration=60, cpuDuration=5, memoryDuration=10 GET /worker/cpu_profile?duration=60 -> passes validation GET /worker/cpu_profile?duration=61 -> HTTP 400 "duration must be between 1 and 60 seconds, got: 61" GET /worker/cpu_profile?duration=0 -> HTTP 400 GET /worker/cpu_profile?duration=abc -> HTTP 400 "duration query parameter must be an integer" RAY_DASHBOARD_PROFILING_MAX_DURATION_S=120 -> maxDuration=120 ``` **Frontend — verified locally:** ``` cd python/ray/dashboard/client ./node_modules/.bin/tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json # 0 errors CI=true npx react-scripts test --testPathPattern=ProfilingLink --watchAll=false # Test Suites: 1 passed, 1 total # Tests: 11 passed, 11 total ./node_modules/.bin/eslint src/common/ProfilingLink*.tsx # clean ./node_modules/.bin/prettier --check src/common/ProfilingLink*.tsx # clean ``` The frontend tests assert, among other things, that the worker Stack Trace link produces `worker/traceback?...&native=1&subprocesses=0` (reflecting a configured `native` default), that it **never emits a hardcoded `native=0`**, and that an out-of-range duration disables submit with an inline error. `pre-commit run --files <changed>` passes (ruff, black, pydoclint, docstyle, import-order, eslint, semgrep). ## Notes for reviewers - All new endpoints/parameters stay behind the existing `RAY_DASHBOARD_ENABLE_PROFILING` security gate — unchanged. - `jax_profile` is deliberately **not** migrated to the shared `_query_duration` helper. It has never enforced a duration cap, and routing it through the shared validator would newly reject durations above the cap for JAX users — a behavior change unrelated to this PR's goal. Its docstring is accurate as-is. - `ProfilingLink.tsx` keeps its own copy of the format lists for the dropdown options, since the frontend can't import the Python constants. Plumbing them through `/api/profiling_enabled` would be a reasonable follow-up.

signal.title: [core][dashboard] Return 4xx from node and actor detail APIs
signal.text: ## Description Makes three node/actor dashboard endpoints report client errors with 4xx status codes instead of 200/500. [#51417](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/51417) added the `HTTPStatusCode` enum and the `rest_response(status_code=...)` plumbing, but adoption stalled after one endpoint. Across non-test dashboard source there are currently 28 `OK` and 13 `INTERNAL_ERROR` usages versus only 4 non-500 error codes, all confined to `state_head.py` / `state_api_utils.py`. Backend (`python/ray/dashboard/modules/node/node_head.py`): - `GET /nodes/{node_id}` returned **200 with a near-empty payload** for an unknown node ID, because `DataOrganizer.get_node_info` falls back to `.get(node_id, {})`. Now returns **404**. - `GET /logical/actors/{actor_id}` returned **200 with `detail: null`** for an unknown actor ID, because `get_actor_infos` maps unknown IDs to `None`. Now returns **404**. - `GET /nodes` with an unsupported `view` returned **500**. An unsupported query parameter is a client error, so it now returns **400**. ## Related issues Related to [#51442](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/51442) (umbrella: revisit Ray dashboard API status codes). Since that issue is an umbrella, this PR covers `node_head.py` only, so each module can be reviewed independently. ## Additional information ### Frontend change is required, not incidental The node and actor detail pages surfaced these cases by reading `result === false` out of the **200 response body**. axios rejects on 4xx, so those branches go dead the moment the status code changes, and the pages would sit on "Loading the node infos..." indefinitely with `msg` never updated. The SWR fetchers in `useNodeDetail.ts` and `useActorDetail.ts` now catch the 404 and set the same message they set before, preserving existing UI behavior. Consumers of `useFetchActor` (the Serve pages) already use optional chaining on the result, so returning `undefined` there is unchanged behavior. ### Tests Added `test_node_api_status_codes` (single cluster, looping over all three error paths plus the three success paths — not parametrized, since `ray_start_with_dashboard` starts a fresh cluster per invocation) and `test_actor_not_found_status_code`. Test environment: because Ray's core is compiled, these were run against the Ray Windows nightly wheel built from `3fb63d965f` — the exact base commit of this branch — with the patched `node_head.py` overlaid, so the patch was the only delta. ``` pytest -v python/ray/dashboard/modules/node/tests/test_node.py -k test_node_api_status_codes 6 passed in 122.16s pytest -v python/ray/dashboard/modules/node/tests/test_actor.py -k test_actor_not_found_status_code 1 passed in 19.74s pytest -q python/ray/dashboard/modules/node/tests/test_actor.py 5 passed in 142.51s pytest -q python/ray/dashboard/modules/node/tests/test_node.py 7 passed, 4 skipped, 2 failed in 286.73s ``` The two failures in the full `test_node.py` run are `test_node_info` and `test_worker_pids_reported`. Both **fail identically against unpatched `node_head.py`** and are pre-existing Windows-environment issues, not regressions: worker cmdlines don't match `"ray::Actor"` on Windows, and runtime_env's uv virtualenv setup hits `WinError 206` (path length). Control run confirming the new tests are not vacuous — against unpatched code: - `/nodes/{unknown}` → `assert 200 == 404` (fails) - `/nodes?view=unknown_view` → `assert 500 == 400` (fails) - `/nodes` → `assert 500 == 400` (fails) - the three success paths → still pass - actor test → `assert 200 == 404`, body `{"result": true, "msg": "Actor details fetched.", "data": {"detail": null}}` (fails) Frontend checks: ``` npx tsc --noEmit # clean, exit 0 npx eslint # clean npx prettier -c # clean ``` Python lint: `ruff check` clean; `black` leaves the changed files unmodified. Caveats worth reviewer attention: all of the above ran on Windows rather than Ray's Linux CI, and against a nightly wheel plus overlaid file rather than a from-source build. Linux CI remains the authoritative check. ### Not a duplicate No open PR references [#51442](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/51442), and the issue timeline has no cross-referenced PRs. The issue has been assigned since 2025-03-18 with no linked work; I commented on it before starting ([comment](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/51442#issuecomment-5084257594)). ### AI assistance AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to produce this change.

signal.title: [Core][Data][CoreWorker]Discussion: remaining gRPC thread amplification with many task workers per node
signal.text: ### Description ## What happened + What you expected to happen We are investigating unexpectedly high native thread counts in Ray Data task workers on Ray **2.55.1**. Ray has already made several improvements related to worker thread counts: - #54988 / #36936 added `RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads`, allowing Raylet to pass a gRPC internal CPU-count hint to worker processes. - #58771 / #58351 introduced `RAY_core_worker_num_server_call_thread` and reduced the default CoreWorker gRPC reply executor to 2 threads. - #63685 later added cgroup-aware CPU sizing for several RayConfig-based thread pools. These changes are helpful. However, in our workload, a high worker-density node can still accumulate a large number of process-local gRPC-related threads. This issue is not requesting that CoreWorkers share a single RPC endpoint. We understand that each CoreWorker needs an independent endpoint for worker-to-worker direct calls, actor/task RPC, and process-level failure isolation. Our concern is the node-level multiplication effect: ```text number of worker processes × per-worker gRPC/runtime thread count ``` When a high-core node runs many one-CPU worker processes, each process brings its own gRPC runtime and associated native threads. Even after applying the existing worker gRPC CPU hint, the aggregate Pod-level thread count remains high. ## Environment - Ray version: `2.55.1` - Workload: Ray Data task workers - One worker Pod - Pod resources: `50 CPU / 500 GB memory` - Normal Ray task workers: `num_cpus=1` - Concurrent task workers: approximately `49` - Workload concurrency, input size, and Pod resource configuration were held constant across experiments. ## Measurements We sampled representative worker processes and grouped native threads by Linux thread name. | Configuration | `event_engine` threads | `nexting_thread` threads | Total threads per representative worker | Peak Pod thread count | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Default | 32 | 16 | ~341 | ~7200 | | `RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads=4` | 20 | 2 | ~115 | ~5800 | The setting reduced peak Pod thread count by approximately **19%**. We did not observe an obvious throughput or latency regression in this workload. The thread-name counts above were collected from the operating system. We would appreciate confirmation of the exact gRPC / Ray components corresponding to the observed names, especially `event_engine` and `nexting_thread`. For example, the thread names were collected with commands similar to: ```bash ps -L -p <pid> -o tid,comm ``` or: ```bash for task in /proc/<pid>/task/*; do cat "$task/comm" done | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr ``` ## Relevant configuration path Our understanding of the current worker-side configuration path is: ```text RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads ↓ Raylet worker startup ↓ RAY_num_grpc_internal_threads in the spawned worker environment ↓ Ray-patched gRPC CPU-count detection ↓ gRPC internal runtime / EventEngine sizing ``` We also understand that the CoreWorker server-call reply executor is separately controlled by: ```text RAY_core_worker_num_server_call_thread ``` and defaults to a small value in current Ray versions. This appears to be an important improvement, but it seems to cover the CoreWorker server-call reply executor rather than all possible gRPC EventEngine/runtime thread sources. ## Why this matters For a high-core node with many one-CPU worker processes, the per-process overhead can still become significant at node level. For illustration, consider a hypothetical 192-CPU node running approximately 192 worker processes. Using the observed thread-name counts above: ```text Default: 192 × (32 event_engine + 16 nexting_thread) ≈ 9216 threads ``` With the reduced gRPC CPU hint: ```text RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads=4: 192 × (20 event_engine + 2 nexting_thread) ≈ 4224 threads ``` These are not exact predictions for every workload or deployment, but they show the multiplication effect. Even mostly idle native threads consume operational budget through: - PID / cgroup `pids.max` usage; - native thread stack reservation and memory overhead; - scheduler overhead; - thread startup and teardown overhead; - increased risk of `pthread_create` / `EAGAIN` failures. This is especially concerning because related reports have already observed worker startup or thread creation failures on high-core systems: - #48700 - #54225 - #59626 ## What we tried We set the following before starting Ray workers: ```bash export RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads=4 ``` This materially reduced worker and Pod thread count without an obvious workload-level performance regression. However, this setting changes a gRPC CPU-count hint rather than expressing a direct worker thread budget. It is therefore difficult for us to know: - whether it is intended as a supported production tuning interface; - which exact gRPC components it changes; - whether it limits initial thread creation only or also runtime growth; - and what values are expected to be safe for different workload types. ## Discussion We would appreciate feedback from Ray maintainers and the community on how this behavior is intended to work and how it should be approached. We understand that each CoreWorker needs an independent RPC endpoint and process-level isolation. We are not assuming that worker processes should necessarily share a single RPC endpoint or that there is one simple solution for all workloads. Our main concern is the node-level multiplication effect: when a high-core node runs many one-CPU worker processes, each process brings its own gRPC runtime and related threads. Even after applying the existing worker gRPC CPU hint, the aggregate thread count can remain large. We would like to better understand the current design, expected operating envelope, and the tradeoffs involved. Questions we would especially appreciate help with: 1. Is `RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads` intended to be a supported production tuning knob for worker processes, or should it be considered an internal escape hatch? 2. Can maintainers clarify which thread pools or gRPC subsystems are affected by: - `RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads` - `RAY_core_worker_num_server_call_thread` - `RAY_num_server_call_thread` 3. In particular, does `RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads`: - affect EventEngine initial thread creation; - constrain EventEngine growth; - affect every EventEngine instance in a CoreWorker process; - or affect only some gRPC subsystems? 4. Is there an existing supported way to set a direct per-CoreWorker limit for EventEngine or other gRPC runtime threads, rather than indirectly changing the gRPC CPU-count hint? 5. For high worker-density nodes, are there existing capacity guidelines or tested configurations covering: - one or approximately one worker per CPU; - high-core hosts; - many Ray Data task workers in a single Pod; - expected worker and Pod thread counts; - `pids.max`, `ulimit -u`, and native-thread stack considerations? 6. Does the cgroup-aware CPU sizing work from #63685 also apply to the CPU count seen by the patched gRPC runtime in workers? If not, is that an area where the current behavior could be improved? Potential areas for discussion might include: - clearer documentation and observability for the existing worker-side thread controls; - a direct per-worker gRPC / EventEngine thread limit; - more conservative defaults for CPU-count-driven gRPC internals in task workers; - a per-node budget or admission mechanism for worker-side RPC threads; - automatic sizing that considers cgroup limits and worker density; - or, where compatible with process isolation and fault-tolerance requirements, consolidation or sharing of selected transport/event-loop resources. We are not proposing a specific architecture here. We would like to understand which directions are technically realistic and aligned with Ray's design goals. ## Willingness to contribute We are happy to help investigate and validate this. If there is a preferred benchmark, diagnostic format, or specific hypothesis the community would like tested, we would be happy to run it and report the results. ## Additional measurements we can provide We can provide the same workload and thread-name breakdown for a matrix such as: ```text default RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads=1 RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads=2 RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads=4 RAY_core_worker_num_server_call_thread=1 RAY_core_worker_num_server_call_thread=2 RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads=4 RAY_core_worker_num_server_call_thread=1 ``` We can also compare the results across Ray versions, including a version that contains #63685. ## Related issues and PRs Issues: - #36936 — Too many threads in Ray worker - #48700 — Ray crashes when too many cores are visible - #54225 — Thread creation error, even with environment variables all set to 1 - #55215 — Make third party library thread count static in worker - #58351 — Same actor/task has different number of threads in different environments - #59626 — Resource exhaustion / `pthread_create` failures in a Ray workload - #63476 — Default GCS thread number considers cgroup Pull requests: - #54988 — Configurable worker gRPC internal thread count - #58771 — Limit CoreWorker gRPC reply threads to 2 by default - #63685 — Consider cgroup limit when fetching CPU ### Use case _No response_

signal.title: [serve] Recover gang context for orphaned replicas to restart the whole gang
signal.text: ## Description When a Serve controller crashes between actor creation and the first `initialize_and_get_metadata` call for a gang member, the orphaned actor lives with `_rank = None` and `_gang_context = None`. #63139 drops the orphan on recovery, but for gang deployments dropping only the orphan leaves surviving siblings with stale `member_replica_ids` references to the dead orphan, splitting the gang. ## Approach Pass `gang_context` to the replica constructor so the actor carries its gang identity from `__init__`, and add a `get_initial_gang_context` RPC that the controller probes during recovery alongside `was_initialized`. The recovered gang_id flows into `failed_gang_ids`, so the existing sibling-cleanup loop force-stops the whole gang in the same reconcile pass leading to atomic restart and no partial gangs. ## Related issues Closes https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/63153. ## Additional information > Optional: Add implementation details, API changes, usage examples, screenshots, etc.

signal.title: [Data] Add task-based shuffle v2 support for sort
signal.text: ## Description This PR adds task-based shuffle v2 support for `Dataset.sort()`. Previously, sort continued to use the legacy `AllToAllOperator` path when `DataContext.shuffle_strategy` was set to `ShuffleStrategy.HASH_SHUFFLE_V2`. This PR routes sort through the task-based shuffle v2 operators: ```text Input -> SortShuffleMapOp -> ShuffleReduceOp ``` `SortShuffleMapOp` extends `ShuffleMapOp` with range-boundary sampling: 1. Validate the sort key schema and buffer all incoming input bundles. 2. Wait for the upstream operator to finish so every input block contributes to boundary selection. 3. Sample every block with bounded task concurrency based on the available CPU parallelism. 4. Reuse sort v1's sample budget and boundary calculation. 5. Replay the buffered inputs through `ShuffleMapOp` for local sorting and range partitioning. ## Local benchmark Benchmark: ```text release/nightly_tests/dataset/sort_benchmark.py ``` Environment: ```text OS: Ubuntu CPU: Intel Core Ultra 7 265K Physical cores: 20 Threads per core: 1 Runs per configuration: 3 ``` Results are averages over three runs: | Input | Partitions | Legacy time | v2 time | Runtime delta | Legacy object-store peak | v2 object-store peak | Memory delta | Legacy spill | v2 spill | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 5.96 GiB | 64 | 6.401 s | 9.243 s | +44.4% | 12.106 GB | 6.002 GB | -50.4% | 0 GB | 0 GB | | 11.92 GiB | 128 | 20.076 s | 14.377 s | -28.4% | 24.155 GB | 11.989 GB | -50.4% | 27.034 GB | 0 GB | ## Additional information This PR does not change the public `Dataset.sort()` API. The new execution path remains opt-in through `DataContext.shuffle_strategy`.

signal.title: [Data] Style and grammar pass on the Ray Data shuffle pages
signal.text: ## Summary Style and grammar pass across the Ray Data shuffle pages, measured against `doc/source/ray-contribute/writing-style.md`. Originally scoped to `data-internals.rst`; extended after #65372 merged so the shuffle v2 content it introduced gets the same treatment as the rest of the page, along with the sibling pages that reference it. No behavior claims are changed. Where a wording fix would have restated a technical claim I couldn't verify, I left the original text alone. ## Rendering fix `joining-data.rst` had three join-type lists written as: ```rst **Semi Joins:** - Left Semi, Right Semi (returns all rows ... ``` RST needs a blank line before a bullet list, so all three rendered as run-together paragraphs with literal `-` characters rather than lists. Confirmed with docutils before and after. ## Style fixes - **Sentence-case headings** throughout. Nothing catches these: `Google.Headings` is disabled repo-wide. - **Feature-stage casing.** "currently in Alpha" to "in alpha", per the guide's rule that Ray-owned stages are lowercase. - **Time-relative words.** Dropped "currently"; replaced the "this is a new feature released in Ray 2.46" note, since 2.46 is no longer new. - **Units.** "100 KB" to 100 KiB and "8 KB" to 8 KiB in `data-internals.rst`, matching the actual `100 * 1024` and `8192` values. The same section already said 1 GiB correctly. - **Bold-as-heading** to definition-list form for the two shuffle v2 tuning settings. - **`export`** added to the `RAY_DATA_DEFAULT_SHUFFLE_STRATEGY` snippet, and the variable named in the lead-in, so the snippet does what the prose describes. - **Wording.** "knobs" to "settings", "only applies" to "applies only", "group-bys" to "group-by operations", one spelling of "trade-off". - **Mechanical.** Unicode quotes and apostrophes, trailing whitespace, comma splices, missing terminal periods, and single backticks where surrounding text uses double. ## Note for reviewers Sentence-casing headings changes their generated HTML anchors, so any external deep link to, for example, `#basic-aggregations` still resolves but `#Custom-Aggregations`-style links to the old casing would not. `autosectionlabel` isn't enabled and every `:ref:` on these pages uses an explicit label, so no in-tree cross-reference breaks. Happy to revert the heading changes if the anchor churn isn't worth it. ## Follow-up status The factual corrections these pages needed shipped separately in #65525, which is merged. That covered the `DataContext.shuffle_strategy` assignment in `saving-data.rst`, the `partition_size_hint` deprecation, and the aggregator-count default in `joining-data.rst`. This branch is merged up with master and carries those corrections, with the `partition_size_hint` bullet's inline literals normalized to double backticks to match the rest of the page. Nothing factual is outstanding.

signal.title: [WIP]: Add writable cgroups guide
signal.text: ## Description Add a KubeRay user guide documenting how to enable Ray resource isolation (`--enable-resource-isolation`) on non-GKE containerd Kubernetes clusters using an NRI (Node Resource Interface) plugin. The plugin selectively grants writable cgroup access to annotated Ray pods without requiring privileged containers. The `nsdelegate` mount option on the node's root cgroup provides the kernel-enforced security boundary. The guide has two tracks: 1. Manual, step-by-step node setup, intended for cluster administrators 1. A non-production quick-start guide intended for AI developers wanting to use Ray with resource isolation on Kubernetes. Both tracks culminate in deploying a RayCluster with `enable-resource-isolation: "true"` and verifying that Ray creates its cgroup hierarchy inside unprivileged containers. ## Related issues <!-- Related to https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/ insert issue number if one exists --> ## Additional information - The NRI plugin source lives at https://github.com/pmengelbert/nri-writable-cgroups. - The annotation key (`writable-cgroups.nri.io/enable`) is configurable via the plugin's `--annotation-key` flag. - The existing GKE-specific writable-cgroups guide is unchanged; this guide targets clusters without GKE's built-in `writableCgroups` feature. - Validated on AKS. Expected outputs are included but have not been verified on EKS or other platforms. - `nsdelegate` remount does not persist across reboots; this is documented as a known limitation.

signal.title: [docs] Sync the vendored KubeRay CRD API reference
signal.text: ## Why are these changes needed? Refreshes the generated KubeRay CRD API reference at `doc/source/cluster/kubernetes/references/api.md` from `ray-project/kuberay` release tag v1.7.0, pinned at commit [`97509c3`](https://github.com/ray-project/kuberay/blob/97509c3a7216cf3440af381646560a1885afb53b/docs/reference/api.md). Opened automatically. The upstream file is a build artifact that `elastic/crd-ref-docs` generates from the Go CRD types in `ray-operator/apis/ray/`, and KubeRay's `ray-operator-verify-api-docs` CI job fails on drift between the two, so the content is verified upstream before it reaches here. That job covers `release-*` branches as well as `master`, so a release tag's artifact carries the same guarantee. This syncs from the latest KubeRay *release*, not from `master`. Master carries CRD surface that no release ships, and documenting it here would advertise fields a reader can't use. The `ray.io/v1alpha1` section is stripped on the way in. That API version is deprecated and on a removal runway (ray-project/kuberay#5124), and its cross-links collide with the v1 anchors (ray-project/kuberay#5091). With one package left, the `Packages` index and the `ray.io/v1` heading restate the page's own subject, so both are dropped and the headings under them move up to h2. Sphinx's right-hand page nav lists h2 only, so this is what puts the CRD types in it. Heading text is untouched, so the anchors cross-links resolve against don't move. A page intro replaces the generated package blurb those headings carried, naming the resource types read off the page's own index. Prose that a Go doc comment indented with a tab becomes a list, and the non-breaking hyphen those comments carry becomes an ASCII one. Tab indentation is godoc's code-block convention, so `crd-ref-docs` passes it through and the renderer turns the sentences into a preformatted block. Both belong upstream (ray-project/kuberay#5146) and this step drops out once they're fixed there. ## Checks Content-only: the single changed file is documentation under `doc/`, so the `docs-go` scope guard applies cleanly. The Read the Docs preview build on this PR is the gate — a green build means the regenerated reference still renders and all of its in-page anchors resolve. Nothing else in this PR. If it contains any other change, something is wrong with the sync job.

signal.title: [tune] Drop the stale subkey check from flatten_dict's list branch
signal.text: ## Description `flatten_dict(dt, prevent_delimiter=True, flatten_list=True)` raises `UnboundLocalError` as soon as a value is a list. On master: ```python >>> from ray.tune.utils.util import flatten_dict >>> flatten_dict({"a": [1, 2]}, flatten_list=True) {'a/0': 1, 'a/1': 2} >>> flatten_dict({"a": [1, 2]}, prevent_delimiter=True, flatten_list=True) UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'subkey' where it is not associated with a value ``` The list branch checks `delimiter in subkey`, but `subkey` is bound only by the dict branch's `for subkey, v in value.items()` loop one block above. With no dict processed first in the same pass, the name is unbound. This deletes the check rather than repairing it. `i` comes from `enumerate()`, so `str(i)` is always digits and can never contain the delimiter, which makes any check on it permanently dead. The dict branch keeps its own check, so a delimiter inside a real subkey still raises. Worth noting because it explains why this went unnoticed: the crash is order-dependent. When a dict is flattened earlier in the same pass, `subkey` is left bound and the list branch silently re-checks that unrelated leftover, so `flatten_dict({"d": {"p": 1}, "L": [7, 8]}, prevent_delimiter=True, flatten_list=True)` returns the correct `{'d/p': 1, 'L/0': 7, 'L/1': 8}` today. That stale read can never change a result or raise spuriously either, since the dict branch has already rejected any subkey containing the delimiter, so the crash is the only observable symptom. Scope: no in-repo caller passes both flags today (`ax_search.py` and `bohb_search.py` pass `prevent_delimiter` only, `hyperopt_search.py` passes `flatten_list` only), so this is a latent crash on the public `ray.tune.utils.util.flatten_dict` re-export rather than something breaking a Tune run. `ray/_private/dict.py` is marked `@Deprecated`, so if the preference is to delete the module rather than repair it, say so and I will close this. ## Related issue number None open. ## Additional information Not a duplicate: searched issues and PRs, open and closed. `gh issue list --repo ray-project/ray --search "flatten_dict prevent_delimiter" --state all` returns two unrelated items (#50315, #48500); a full-text search for `flatten_dict` returns 15 hits, the closest being #17241 "[tune] Add test for flatten_dict."; `--search "prevent_delimiter"` returns two unrelated issues and zero PRs; `gh pr list --search "flatten_dict subkey"` returns nothing; `--search "_private/dict.py"` returns only #61632 (Trackio integration) and #42858, neither touching this function. `FlattenDictTest` in `python/ray/tune/tests/test_trainable_util.py` currently has no `prevent_delimiter` coverage at all. Tests run (CPU, macOS, Python 3.11.9, ray 2.56.1 whose `flatten_dict` is AST-identical to master's): - `pytest python/ray/tune/tests/test_trainable_util.py -k FlattenDict` Against unpatched Ray: `1 failed, 12 passed, 5 deselected` (the new `test_flatten_list_with_prevent_delimiter` fails with the `UnboundLocalError` above). With this change: all pass. - `pytest python/ray/tune/tests/test_trainable_util.py` (whole file, with this change): `18 passed`. - The same file at master revision, run against the patched source, as a regression control: `16 passed`, so the fix does not disturb any existing case. The second new test, `test_prevent_delimiter_still_raises_with_flatten_list`, is there to pin the part that must not change: `flatten_dict({"a": {"b/c": 1}}, prevent_delimiter=True, flatten_list=True)` must still raise `ValueError`. It passes both before and after, and is what would catch the deletion going too far. AI assistance was used for this change.

signal.title: [cherry-pick][2.58.0][Fix][Core] Give `canceled_tasks_` its own mutex to break a lock-order cycle (#65393)
signal.text: ## Description Cherry-pick of #65393 (`e3ff26cec3`) into `releases/2.58.0`. The release branch has the cherry-pick of #65184 (`90489021a8`, via #65400), which introduced a mutex lock-order cycle, but is missing the follow-up fix #65393 that breaks the cycle by giving `canceled_tasks_` its own mutex. In debug builds, absl's deadlock detector observes the cycle (`CoreWorker::HandleGetCoreWorkerStats()` → `ReferenceCounter::NumObjectIDsInScope()`) and SIGABRTs the worker. This is deterministically failing the `core: debug tests` job on the release branch postmerge: https://buildkite.com/ray-project/postmerge/builds/19264 — `test_object_spilling{,_2,_3}_debug_mode` and `test_scheduling{,_2}_debug_mode` all abort with `RAW: Potential Mutex deadlock ... a cycle in the historical lock ordering graph has been observed`. The same job passes on master, which has both commits. ## Verification - Clean cherry-pick (`git cherry-pick -x -s e3ff26cec3`), no conflicts; 2 files changed matching the original commit. - Root cause confirmed from the postmerge build 19264 logs: the abort stack matches the exact cycle described in #65393's description, and `releases/2.58.0` still had `canceled_tasks_ ABSL_GUARDED_BY(mutex_)` (pre-fix) while master has the dedicated `canceled_tasks_mutex_`. - The failing `core: debug tests` postmerge job on this branch will validate the fix in CI; the original change passed full CI on master. signal.title: [core][sandbox] Make Ray Sandbox run Docker-built images out of the box
signal.text: ## Description `ray.experimental.sandbox` cannot run standard Docker-built images without reaching for the private `_oci_spec_transform_fn` hook and client-side workarounds. We hit all of these while integrating Ray Sandbox with the [Harbor](https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor) eval framework (see the workarounds carried in harbor-framework/harbor#2725), and the follow-up items while testing this PR end-to-end on a live Ray cluster with real gVisor. ### Capabilities - **`SandboxConfig.capabilities`** (plumbed through `create()`, the `Sandbox` actor, `SandboxRuntime.create`, and the gVisor backend): None keeps the runtime default; otherwise the bounding/effective/permitted sets are written exactly, so `[]` runs with no capabilities at all (inheritable and ambient untouched, matching modern Docker, which stopped setting inheritable for CVE-2022-24769). A new `DOCKER_DEFAULT_CAPABILITIES` constant ([Docker's documented default set](https://docs.docker.com/engine/containers/run/#runtime-privilege-and-linux-capabilities)) gives Docker parity in one line: the runtime's default (whatever `runsc spec` emits) grants only three capabilities, and standard images break confusingly without more — `apt-get` needs `CAP_SETUID`/`CAP_SETGID` for its `_apt` sub-processes, `tar` extracting as root fatally fails restoring archived uid/gids (e.g. `1000`) without `CAP_CHOWN`. ### Networking and DNS - **`network="public"`** — the recommended internet-access mode: host egress (`--network=host` under the hood) with a **synthetic `/etc/resolv.conf`** generated from `dns` (default `8.8.8.8`, `1.1.1.1`). Nothing about the host resolver is inherited, so the config stays portable and doesn't leak host search domains or internal resolver addresses (a cluster node's resolv.conf typically carries internal Kubernetes search domains, the cluster DNS VIP, and `ndots:5`). - **`network="host"`** stays the explicit power mode — full host network identity (including internal networks reachable from the node) with the host's own resolv.conf mounted read-only; `dns=` overrides it with a generated file. Keeping the modes separate lets the docs state that difference plainly. `"none"` remains the default. - **`dns=`** mirrors `docker --dns` and is the escape hatch for locked-down VPCs that block public DNS; it's rejected for modes that mount no resolv.conf. Host-side networking also drops the spec's empty network namespace, which previously left the sandbox loopback-only despite `--network=host`. - **`network="sandbox"` with `rootless=True` is rejected at config time**: runsc refuses the combination at container start, after the image pull, with an error naming a flag the user never set. ### Working directory and writability - **Writability is now fully explicit** — determined by the two parameters the user actually set, with the image's `WORKDIR` inherited for the *process cwd only*: | `readonly` | `workdir` | writable | cwd | |---|---|---|---| | `True` *(default)* | `None` *(default)* | nothing on the rootfs (safe default; standard tmpfs mounts like `/tmp` remain writable) | image `WORKDIR`, else `/` | | `True` | `/data` | only `/data` (host-backed scratch) | `/data` | | `False` | any | everything (per-sandbox overlay; image content stays visible, nothing shadowed) | explicit workdir, else image `WORKDIR` | Previously the backend defaulted `workdir` to the image's `WORKDIR` (or `/`) and scratch-mounted there, so what was writable depended on image metadata invisible in the config. An inherited `WORKDIR` is never silently made writable now. This made the interim `mount_workdir` knob redundant, so it's removed; the backend also no longer mutates `config.workdir` (the resolved cwd lives in sandbox metadata), and inherited image `WORKDIR` values are no longer used in host path joins, removing that traversal surface. ### TTL - **`ttl_seconds` now defaults to `None`** (no TTL) everywhere: the old 1h default was wall-clock from creation, not idle time, so actively-running sandboxes were deleted mid-work — a silent, hard-to-attribute failure in long agent runs. Opt-in destruction is the safer default. - **`SandboxRuntime` now actually enforces a set TTL** (daemon timer, canceled on delete); previously the parameter was a documented no-op below the actor layer, and the `Sandbox` actor's duplicate timer is dropped in favor of the runtime's. ### Shell for string commands - String commands ran under `/bin/sh` — `dash` on Debian-family images — while agent-generated commands overwhelmingly assume bash, failing confusingly on `[[ ]]`/`pipefail`/arrays. **`SandboxConfig.shell`** now defaults to `"/bin/bash"` outright (no auto-detection — deterministic per review), with a per-command `shell=` override on `exec()`. Images without bash set `shell="/bin/sh"` explicitly, as the busybox-based tests now do; list commands still bypass the shell. ### Robustness - `SandboxRuntime.create()` forwards `mount_workdir` into the config (it was silently dropped — caught by live testing; a new runtime-layer test suite pins config fields actually reaching the backend, the gap that let it ship green). - Caller-supplied `base_spec`s with null capability sets or non-dict namespace entries no longer raise; malformed namespace entries are kept for runsc to reject with its own error. - `SandboxConfig` validates the network mode against `("none", "public", "host", "sandbox")`. Defaults are behavior-preserving except where called out (TTL, and mount_workdir under `readonly=False`); the API is alpha. ## Related issues Related to #64964 (Ray Sandboxing with gVisor). Enables removing the OCI-spec transform, DNS seeding, and `tar --no-same-owner` workarounds in harbor-framework/harbor#2725 / harbor-framework/harbor#2785. ## Additional information Usage: ```python from ray.experimental import sandbox from ray.experimental.sandbox import DOCKER_DEFAULT_CAPABILITIES sb = sandbox.create( image="ubuntu:24.04", network="public", capabilities=DOCKER_DEFAULT_CAPABILITIES, readonly=False, ) # apt-get / tar / DNS / bash / image WORKDIR all behave as under Docker, # without inheriting the host's resolver configuration. ``` Testing: - Unit tests run without runsc or a cluster: spec construction against `base_spec` with a stub image manager, config validation, resolv.conf generation policy at the `prepare_oci_bundle` layer, and a new `SandboxRuntime`-layer suite (fake backend) covering field forwarding and TTL enforcement. - Full `TEST_SANDBOX=1` suite with real gVisor/runsc on Linux: 64 tests pass, including the shell-detection and rootless-rejection paths. - Docs: new "Networking and DNS" section with the mode table and security property of each mode, the recommended internet-access example, the `dns=` escape hatch, and an updated OCI-transform section (its example used the now-rejected `network="sandbox"` default combination and hand-mounted resolv.conf). This is the first of two changes for running Harbor evals on Ray Sandbox; a follow-up adds an HTTP API service so sandboxes can be consumed as a standalone service.

signal.title: [Data][LLM] Add multi-host TPU batch inference for Ray Data LLM
signal.text: ## Summary I wrote a design document for this feature [here](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1E6wd-WWl6ahtTd95ngsMBc1UmoYXsvFFm__Nu_ueryk/edit?tab=t.0). This PR adds multi-host TPU support to Ray Data LLM batch inference (`vLLMEngineProcessorConfig` / `build_processor`). With a TPU `accelerator_type` and a topology in `accelerator_config`, each engine actor reserves its own TPU slice placement group and runs on bundle 0 (CPU only, `capture_child_tasks=True`), so the engine's vLLM workers are gang-scheduled onto the slice. Accelerator config/backends live in `python/ray/llm/_internal/common/accelerators.py` and are shared with Serve. Batch scheduling now resolves through `AcceleratorBackend.build_batch_scheduling_options`, so the builder calls the backend unconditionally and `vLLMEngineStage.post_init` is removed. The GPU path keeps its existing behavior (same bundles, same PACK placement group per actor), just built in `GPUAccelerator` instead of the stage. ```python config = vLLMEngineProcessorConfig( model_source="...", accelerator_type="TPU-V6E", accelerator_config={"kind": "tpu", "topology": "4x4"}, # TP * PP * DP must equal topology chip count (PP/DP default to 1). engine_kwargs={"tensor_parallel_size": 16}, ) processor = build_processor(config) out = processor(ds) ``` Both backends build their scheduling strategy in a static `_scheduling_strategy_fn` passed to `ray_remote_args_fn` via `partial`, so Ray Data invokes it once per actor replica. `concurrency > 1` works on TPU: each replica gets its own slice. `chips_per_vm` field is also added for the TPU backend to support ambiguous topologies (v6e `2x4`, etc.). This field is already accepted by `SlicePlacementGroup` so I just added it to the parameters users can specify for TPU in their config. ## Behavior changes - `accelerator_type="CPU"` is rejected for vLLM batch inference - `get_accelerator_backend` raises on unrecognized configs - TPU fill constraint is `tensor_parallel_size * pipeline_parallel_size * data_parallel_size == topology chips` (PP/DP default to 1). This diverges from GPU (`tp*pp` only) because the TPU slice size is fixed by topology and equality must count every device dimension. - TPU slice bundles carry `accelerator_type:<TYPE>: 0.001`, matching Serve's `default_bundles`. This constrains single-host topologies to the requested generation and lets the engine actor admit onto bundle 0. - `build_processor` no longer mutates the caller's `engine_kwargs`; `distributed_executor_backend` is set on a private copy. ## Testing - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration test against a simulated multi-host v6e-16 cluster (real slice PG creation and GCS state) - [x] Manual test - converted a GPU example from ray docs to TPU, process in comments ## Follow-ups - Docs for TPU batch inference - Configurable `DEFAULT_PG_READY_TIMEOUT_S`

signal.title: [serve] Deflake test_gcs_failure GCS restart race
signal.text: This PR addresses yet another flake in test_gcs_failure_with_pack_scheduling. There are two issues, both related to start_gcs_server() test_controller_gcs_failure calls serve.run(d.bind()) immediately after restarting the GCS. A just-restarted GCS is not reachable yet, and the redeploy's checkpoint write runs under the fixture's RAY_SERVE_KV_TIMEOUT_S=1, so the controller can die with "Timed out while waiting for GCS to become available". The only slack was the incidental 4s of the pytest.raises before it. The fix is to wait for the GCS to answer a write first. The serve_ha fixture then turns any such failure into a whole-file outage. Its teardown restarts the GCS unconditionally, correct when the test left it down, but it asserts "GCS server is already running" when a test fails as described above. The fix is to restart only when the GCS is actually down, and always shut down.

signal.title: [Serve] Orphan ProxyActor left ALIVE when proxy shutdown times out under heavy controller load (blocks worker scale-down)
signal.text: ### What happened + What you expected to happen **Bug** On a large Ray Serve cluster (~381 applications / many `DeploymentHandle`s), the Serve controller repeatedly logs: ```text ERROR ... controller ... -- Exception updating proxy state. Traceback (most recent call last): File ".../ray/serve/_private/controller.py", line 607, in run_control_loop_step self.proxy_state_manager.update(proxy_nodes=self._proxy_nodes) File ".../ray/serve/_private/proxy_state.py", line 781, in update self._stop_proxies_if_needed() File ".../ray/serve/_private/proxy_state.py", line 982, in _stop_proxies_if_needed proxy_state.shutdown() File ".../ray/serve/_private/proxy_state.py", line 567, in shutdown self._actor_proxy_wrapper.kill() File ".../ray/serve/_private/proxy_state.py", line 323, in kill ray.get(shutdown_ref, timeout=5) ... ray.exceptions.GetTimeoutError: Get timed out: some object(s) not ready. ``` After this, worker nodes that should be idle keep an **ALIVE** `ProxyActor` that is **no longer tracked** in `serve.status().proxies`. Those orphan proxies prevent the autoscaler from scaling the workers down. **Expected** When the controller decides to stop a proxy, either: 1. the proxy is gracefully shut down and `ray.kill`'d, **or** 2. if `shutdown.remote()` times out / fails, the actor is still force-killed and not left as an unmanaged ALIVE orphan. `serve.status().proxies` and the set of ALIVE Serve `ProxyActor`s should stay consistent. ### Root cause analysis Two bugs compound under controller overload: #### 1) Half-cleanup in stop/kill path (immediate orphan creator) `_stop_proxies_if_needed` removes the proxy from the manager **before** kill completes: ```python # proxy_state.py (_stop_proxies_if_needed) for node_id in to_stop: proxy_state = self._proxy_states.pop(node_id) # (1) drop from managed state ... proxy_state.shutdown() ``` `ActorProxyWrapper.kill()` then does: ```python shutdown_ref = self._actor_handle.shutdown.remote() ray.get(shutdown_ref, timeout=5) # (2) can raise GetTimeoutError ray.kill(self._actor_handle, no_restart=True) # (3) never reached on timeout ``` The controller control loop catches the exception and continues: ```python # controller.py except Exception: logger.exception("Exception updating proxy state.") ``` Result: | Step | Effect | |---|---| | `pop` succeeded | proxy disappears from `status().proxies` | | `ray.get(shutdown, timeout=5)` timed out | exception aborts `kill()` | | `ray.kill` never runs | actor remains **ALIVE** | | controller forgets the actor | **orphan** → blocks worker idle / scale-down | `ProxyActor.shutdown()` itself is essentially a no-op / very cheap; a 5s timeout strongly suggests RPC / scheduling / controller overload rather than heavy shutdown work. #### 2) Control-loop overload with hundreds of apps (trigger) With ~**381 Serve applications** and a large number of `DeploymentHandle`s, the controller control loop is heavily loaded (metrics / long-poll / proxy health+drain+stop bookkeeping). Under that load, `shutdown.remote()` often cannot complete within 5s, so path (1) fires repeatedly and leaves orphan proxies on workers. This matches the direction of ongoing controller scalability work: - https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/64510 — refresh GCS node-info cache off the control loop (async) - https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/64886 — cache merged autoscaling-metrics timeseries across controller ticks - https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/63144 — `[Serve][RFC] Scaling Autoscaling Metrics Communication in Ray Serve` Related but different open PR that also touches the proxy kill/update path: - https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/64403 — fix proxy update loop stuck on `ActorUnschedulableError` in `is_shutdown()` (exception escape / hang). That does **not** cover the `GetTimeoutError` after `pop` leaving an ALIVE orphan. ### Suggested fixes **Hardening (should fix orphans even under load):** 1. In `ActorProxyWrapper.kill()`, always call `ray.kill(..., no_restart=True)` in a `finally` (or after catching `GetTimeoutError` / other Ray errors), so a timed-out graceful shutdown cannot leave an ALIVE actor. 2. Optionally reverse `_stop_proxies_if_needed` ordering: only `pop` after successful kill, or keep a "stopping" tombstone so a failed stop can be retried instead of forgotten. **Scalability (address the overload trigger):** Continue reducing per-tick control-loop work for large app / handle counts (related: #64510, #64886, #63144). ### Workaround Manually kill ALIVE Serve `ProxyActor`s that are not present in `serve.status().proxies`. Reducing app/handle count or using head-only proxy placement also lowers how often this path is hit. ### Versions / Dependencies - Ray **2.55.0** - Python 3.10 - Large Serve footprint: ~381 applications / many DeploymentHandles on one controller - Observed on a production-like large multi-app cluster; stack traces match `proxy_state.py` / `controller.py` on this version ### Reproduction script Fully minimal local repro is hard because it depends on controller overload, but the failure mode is deterministic from the code path: 1. Deploy many Serve applications (hundreds) so the controller control loop is saturated (metrics / long-poll / proxy management). 2. Trigger proxy stop/drain (scale deployments down, or remove replicas from a worker so the proxy becomes drainable / stoppable). 3. Observe controller logs: `Exception updating proxy state.` with `GetTimeoutError` in `ActorProxyWrapper.kill` at `ray.get(shutdown_ref, timeout=5)`. 4. Compare: - `serve.status().proxies` — node missing - `ray list actors` / actor table — corresponding `ProxyActor` still **ALIVE** 5. Autoscaler / KubeRay does not remove the worker because the orphan proxy keeps the node non-idle. A unit-level repro can patch `ray.get` in `ActorProxyWrapper.kill` to raise `GetTimeoutError` and assert that `ray.kill` is still invoked and/or the proxy remains managed for retry. ### Issue Severity High: It blocks me from completing my task. Worker scale-down is blocked until orphan proxies are cleaned up manually; this is painful on large autoscaled clusters.
signal.author: zhangsikai123

signal.title: [serve] Deflake test_recursive_cancellation_during_execution
signal.text: This PR addresses a flake in `test_recursive_cancellation_during_execution` which synchronizes on a fixed 0.5s sleep instead of on the state it requires. `Replica._on_request_cancelled` only cancels child requests that are pending assignment, so the test needs `inner` to be executing when the cancel lands. If `inner` is still pending assignment, its assignment task is torn down, so it never enters `send_signal_on_cancellation`, causing the test to fail with `GetTimeoutError`. Holding the only slot of `inner` to delay its assignment shows the margin is under half a second, the test passes with a 0.1s delay and fails at 0.45s, 1.0s and 2.0s. The fix is to have `inner` signal from inside its cancel-catching block and wait for that before cancelling, the same method that `test_cancel_sync_handle_call_during_execution` already uses. Its three `ray.get` waits also go from 10s to 20s. Test-only change.
